There’s something very comforting and cosy about Christmas drinks. From Christmas punch, boozy hot chocolates to a bit of fizz - what more can you ask for during the festive season?

Drinks House 247 have put together 10 easy Christmas drinks for you to make, whether you’re hosting for the day or you need to wind down after seeing the family.

Christmas Punch

Start Christmas day off with a bang with some Christmas punch. A fruity blend of pomegranate, lime, and cranberry with the added splash of fizz to get the party started.

Our ingredients serve 4 people.

Ingredients

  • 1 litre of cranberry juice
  • 1 litre of soda water
  • 1 litre of lime cordial
  • 100ml of prosecco
  • Cranberries, lime and mint to garnish

Method

  1. Put the cranberry juice, soda water and lime cordial into a jug and stir until combined.
  2. Add the prosecco and stir gradually.
  3. Garnish with cranberries, lime and mint and then serve.

Pear and Rosemary Gin Fizz

Add a touch of fizz to your Christmas drinks with this pear and rosemary gin. Our ingredients serve 2 people.

Ingredients

  • 100ml of Gin
  • 50ml of pear juice
  • 50ml of soda water
  • Juice of a lemon, plus slices to serve
  • Rosemary sprig

Method

  1. Fill 2 glasses with ice and pour the gin and pear juice together.
  2. Add a good squeeze of lemon and the rosemary sprig.
  3. Top with soda water before serving.

Sugar Cookie Martini

Sweet and delicious, this Sugar Cookie Martini will be your favourite easy Christmas drink to make. Our ingredients, serve 2 people.

Ingredients

  • 200ml of whole milk
  • 100ml of Baileys
  • 100ml of Vodka
  • 100ml of Amaretto (You can swap this for White Chocolate Liqueur if preferred)
  • Ice
  • Buttercream and sprinkles to garnish

Method

  1. Dip 2 Martini glasses into the buttercream, and then dip again into the sprinkles to decorate the rim of the glass.
  2. In a cocktail shaker, combine the milk, Baileys, vodka, and amaretto or white chocolate liqueur. Add the ice and shake until it’s combined and cold.
  3. Pour in your glasses and enjoy!

White Christmas Mojito

Did you think Mojitos were only for summer? Think again! This Christmas blend is extremely coco-nutty, so if you don’t like coconut, skip to the next easy Christmas drink recipe. Our ingredients serve 2 people.

Ingredients

  • 50ml of White Rum
  • 50ml of Malibu
  • ½ a can of coconut milk
  • 1 tsp of sugar
  • Juice of a lime
  • Mint leaves
  • Sparkling water to serve

Method

  1. In a glass, pour the lime juice, sugar, and mint leaves together and stir until the leaves have broken down.
  2. Fill the glass halfway with ice.
  3. In a blender, combine the white rum, Malibu and coconut milk and pulse until smooth.
  4. Pour over the ice and stir well to combine.
  5. Top with sparkling water and garnish with any leftover mint leaves.

Holiday Peppermint White Russian

If you aren’t in the holiday spirit, this Peppermint White Russian is bound to get you feeling festive. Our ingredients serve 2 people.

Ingredients

  • 100ml of Vodka
  • 100ml of coffee liqueur
  • 100ml of peppermint schnapps
  • 2 tsp of granulated sugar
  • 250ml of milk
  • Ice
  • Crushed candy canes
  • 2 whole candy canes to garnish

Method

  1. Combine the crushed candy canes and granulated sugar in a small bowl and mix well.
  2. Fill a cocktail shaker with peppermint schnapps, coffee liqueur, vodka, and ice.
  3. Shake well until combined and cold.
  4. Pour into 2 glasses and top with a desired amount of milk.
  5. Garnish with candy canes if desired.

Chocolate Orange Cocktail

Are you a fan of chocolate orange? How about in a cocktail? Our ingredients serve 4 people.

Ingredients

  • 100ml of Vodka
  • 100ml of chocolate liqueur
  • 50ml of orange syrup
  • 50ml of orange juice
  • Orange zest
  • 100g of caster sugar
  • Ice
  • Grated chocolate to garnish

Method

  1. To make the orange syrup, combine 100ml of water with the caster sugar and orange zest into a pan and bring to a boil.
  2. Strain this and cool.
  3. Chill 4 Martini glasses and dampen the rim with a little water, and then dip in grated chocolate to decorate.
  4. In a cocktail shaker, combine the vodka, chocolate liqueur, orange syrup, orange juice and ice together.
  5. Shake well and pour into the glasses.
﻿

Salted Caramel Espresso Martini

This easy Christmas drink is the perfect combination for lovers of Espresso Martinis and has a sweet tooth. Our ingredients serve 2 people.

Ingredients

  • 100ml of Vodka
  • 50ml of coffee liqueur
  • 50ml of espresso
  • 1 tsp of caramel
  • Grated chocolate to serve
  • Ice

Method

  1. Place the caramel, espresso and a pinch of salt into a cocktail shaker and stir until the caramel has dissolved.
  2. Add the coffee liquor and vodka and top with ice.
  3. Shake until combined and it becomes frothy.
  4. Strain the mixture and divide between two chilled Martini glasses, and top with grated chocolate to serve.

Mulled Cider

You can’t beat a nice mug of mulled cider after finishing your Christmas shopping. Follow our easy Christmas drinks recipe, and you’ll not be disappointed. Our ingredients serve 2 people.

Ingredients

  • 440ml of Cider
  • 100ml of Whiskey
  • 200ml of apple juice
  • 50g of dark brown sugar
  • Orange zest
  • 2 cinnamon stick
  • 1 tsp of berries

Method

  1. Pour the cider, brandy, apple juice and sugar into a saucepan and gently heat to mull.
  2. Add the orange zest and berries and simmer for 20-30 minutes.
  3. Ladle into glass mugs to serve.

Hot Buttered Rum

Getting snow at Christmas might not be guaranteed, but having a cup of cheer is definitive with this hot buttered rum easy Christmas drink. Our ingredients serve 2 people.

Ingredients

  • 100ml of Dark Rum
  • 2 tsp of butter
  • 2 tsp of brown sugar
  • 1 tsp of vanilla extract
  • Pinch of cinnamon, nutmeg & allspice
  • 200ml of hot water
  • Cinnamon stick to garnish

Method

  1. Place the sugar, butter, vanilla extract and spices into the bottom of a coffee glass or mug and mix thoroughly.
  2. Pour in the rum and top it up with hot water.
  3. Stir well and garnish with a cinnamon stick.

Luscious Baileys Hot Chocolate

Is it even Christmastime without a boozy hot chocolate? Cosy on up by the fire with our luscious Baileys Hot Chocolate. Our ingredients serve 2 people.

Ingredients

  • 8 tsp of hot chocolate powder
  • 400ml of milk
  • 100ml of Baileys
  • Marshmallows for topping
  • Whipped cream for topping

Method

  1. Add the milk into a saucepan and place over medium heat.
  2. Put the hot chocolate powder into two large mugs and divide the hot milk between them.
  3. Pour the Baileys into the hot chocolates and top with whipped cream and marshmallows.

Whiskey Eggnog

Traditional eggnog is great but can take a while to make. We’ve put together a quicker version that is just as tasty and can be enjoyed warm or over ice. Our ingredients serve 2 people.

Ingredients

  • 100ml of Whiskey
  • 500ml of vanilla ice cream
  • 1 tsp of vanilla extract
  • 1 tsp of ginger, cinnamon and nutmeg

Method

Warm:

  1. Warm the ice cream in a saucepan over medium heat and bring to a simmer.
  2. Combine the remaining ingredients and divide between glasses.
  3. Top with the spices and serve.

Chilled:

  1. Alternatively, you can serve chilled over ice.
  2. Combine all the ingredients except the ice and nutmeg into a blender and whisk until smooth.
  3. Transfer to a larger screw-top jar with a lid, add the ice, seal and shake well until combined.
  4. Strain into glasses and scatter the nutmeg to serve.

Five End of Summer Cocktails Worth Making Now

There is a specific fortnight at the end of August when the drinks that carried you through July stop quite working. The light goes earlier, the evenings develop an edge, and a glass of something bright and citrus-heavy feels a little thin. Good end of summer cocktails acknowledge that shift rather than ignoring it. They keep the length and the ice, because it is still warm enough to want both, but they move the flavour towards darker fruit, orchard fruit and herbs.

These five are all easy to make at home, all use ingredients you can actually buy, and all give exact measures rather than vague instructions to add a splash of something.

Blackberry and Thyme Gin Sour

Blackberries hit their proper season in late August and are the single best marker of the turn. This is a Bramble variant with the sweetness pulled back.

Muddle four blackberries and a sprig of thyme in the base of a shaker. Add 50ml gin, 25ml fresh lemon juice and 12.5ml sugar syrup. Shake hard with ice, then strain into a rocks glass filled with crushed ice. Garnish with a blackberry and a bruised thyme sprig.

The thyme is what makes it seasonal rather than simply fruity. Bruise it between your palms before it goes in, otherwise it contributes nothing. A juniper-forward London Dry works better here than a floral contemporary gin, because you want the botanicals to push against the fruit. The spirits range covers both styles.

Apple and Rum Highball

Cloudy apple juice is the most underused mixer in a British kitchen and it is exactly right for the end of August.

Fill a tall glass to the top with ice. Add 50ml white or lightly aged rum, 15ml fresh lime juice, then top with roughly 100ml cloudy apple juice. Stir once, gently, and garnish with a thin apple slice.

The lime is not optional. Apple juice on its own is flabby and sweet, and the acidity is what turns it into a drink rather than a soft drink with rum in it. If you want more structure, use a dark rum instead and add two dashes of bitters.

Peach and Prosecco Long Drink

A Bellini is a lovely thing and a poor party drink, because it needs peach puree and goes warm in five minutes. This is the version that works when you are pouring for eight people.

Slice one ripe peach and muddle it with 15ml lemon juice and 10ml sugar syrup in a jug. Multiply by the number of servings, leave it in the fridge for an hour, then strain into wine glasses over one large ice cube and top each with 100ml chilled prosecco.

Using a wine glass over ice rather than a flute is the whole trick. It keeps the drink cold for longer, it makes the fruit aroma readable, and it stops the drink from being finished in three mouthfuls. If the peaches are underripe, use tinned peaches in juice rather than a poor fresh one.

Rosemary Paloma

Tequila belongs to summer, but a Paloma with a herbal note carries into September in a way that a straightforward Margarita does not.

Put a rosemary sprig in a highball glass and press it once against the side with a spoon. Add ice, 50ml blanco tequila, 20ml fresh lime juice and 10ml sugar syrup, then top with about 100ml grapefruit soda or grapefruit juice and soda in equal parts. A pinch of salt genuinely improves it and is worth doing.

Grapefruit is the bridge flavour here. It has summer brightness but also a bitterness that suits cooler air, and it stops the drink reading as a holiday cocktail once the weather turns.

Whisky, Soda and Lemon

The simplest drink on this list and the one most likely to surprise people. A whisky highball is genuinely refreshing, considerably lighter than it sounds, and it is the natural bridge from summer drinking into autumn.

Fill a tall glass completely with ice, which matters more than usual here. Add 50ml blended Scotch, then top with 150ml well-chilled soda water. Stir exactly once, from the bottom up, then express a lemon peel over the surface and drop it in.

Do not stir it repeatedly, which knocks the carbonation out, and do not use a lightly filled glass, because half-empty ice melts faster and dilutes the drink. A blended whisky works better than a heavily peated single malt in this format.

Getting the Practical Bits Right

Three things separate a decent home cocktail from a good one, and none involves expensive equipment. Use fresh citrus, always, because bottled juice is cooked and tastes of it. Make sugar syrup by dissolving equal weights of sugar and hot water and keeping it in a bottle in the fridge, where it lasts a month. And use far more ice than feels reasonable, since a full glass of ice melts more slowly than a half-full one and dilutes the drink less.

If you are making these for a group, batch the spirit, citrus and syrup together in advance and keep everything sparkling separate until the moment of pouring. A pre-mixed case is worth a look if you would rather not shop for five different bottles, and the wine and prosecco range covers the fizz.

Price matters more, provenance matters more, and the gap between a smart purchase and an underwhelming one can be wide. The good news is that you do not need to be a collector to buy confidently. You need a clear reason for buying, a basic handle on quality signals, and enough discipline not to overpay for the wrong name.

What a fine wine buying guide should help you decide

Start with purpose, not prestige. Are you buying to drink soon, to cellar, to gift, or to mark an occasion? The right answer changes everything from region to vintage to bottle format.

If the bottle is for near-term drinking, balance and readiness matter more than theoretical ageing potential. A mature Rioja Reserva, a well-made Burgundy with a few years behind it, or a serious Barolo from a more approachable vintage may give more pleasure now than a very young trophy bottle that still needs time. If it is for storage, structure becomes more important. Acidity, tannin, concentration and producer track record all matter because they point to how the wine may develop.

For gifting, recognisable regions and estates often carry more weight than obscure brilliance. A recipient may appreciate a top producer from the Northern Rhône, but a classic Bordeaux, fine Champagne or a respected Burgundy label is usually easier to place and easier to present. Fine wine buying is not only about what is best in a critic's glass. It is also about what works for the person receiving it.

Price, rarity and value are not the same thing

One of the biggest mistakes in any fine wine buying guide is treating expensive as automatically superior. Price can reflect scarcity, fashion, critic attention, import levels and branding as much as pure quality. That does not mean prestige wines are not worth buying. It means you should know what you are paying for.

Some regions command a premium because the top vineyard land is tiny and globally recognised. Burgundy is the obvious example. The upside is exceptional nuance at the highest level. The downside is that entry into sought-after names can be costly, and value can disappear fast if demand spikes. Bordeaux often offers a broader value ladder. You can still find classically structured wines from good producers at prices below the headline labels.

Outside France, Italy and Spain can be especially strong for buyers who want pedigree without maximum hype. Barolo, Brunello di Montalcino, top Rioja and Super Tuscans all have their place, but their value varies by producer and vintage. A lesser-known estate in a strong year can outperform a famous name in a weaker one.

How to assess a bottle before you buy

Producer comes first. In fine wine, who made it usually tells you more than a glossy label. Strong producers tend to perform consistently across vintages and quality levels. Even in difficult years, disciplined vineyard work and careful winemaking can protect quality.

Vintage is the next filter, but it should be used properly. A strong vintage can mean ripeness, concentration and longevity, though style still varies by estate. A cooler or more challenging year is not always one to avoid. Sometimes it produces fresher, more classic wines that suit traditional drinkers better. If you are buying to drink now, a less monumental vintage can actually be more convenient.

Storage and provenance matter most when the wine has age. A fine bottle that has been badly stored is still a bad bottle. Look for signs that suggest proper handling: intact labels, sound capsules, sensible fill levels on older bottles and a retailer that takes condition seriously. This is especially relevant for vintage wines and large-format bottles, where replacement is not always easy.

Fine wine regions worth knowing

You do not need a map of every appellation in Europe, but a few anchor regions help you buy faster. Bordeaux remains a cornerstone for collectors and gift buyers because it offers recognisable names, left bank Cabernet structure, right bank Merlot richness and a wide range of price points. Burgundy is more delicate, site-driven and often more expensive, with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay at its core.

Champagne belongs in the fine wine conversation too. Prestige cuvées, vintage expressions and grower producers can all make strong purchases depending on your budget and occasion. For celebration gifting, Champagne often wins on impact before the cork is even out.

Italy gives you stylistic range. Barolo offers tannic structure and ageing potential. Brunello brings depth and polish. Amarone adds power and richness. Spain, especially Rioja and Ribera del Duero, can offer mature, complex wines that are ready to drink earlier than buyers expect. If you want precision and freshness, top German Riesling and serious Loire whites deserve attention. If you want collectible New World names, look to benchmark producers from Napa, Australia and Chile, but buy selectively because prices can climb quickly.

When to buy for drinking, cellaring or gifting

The best buying decision often comes down to timing. If a bottle is needed for a dinner this week, buying a tightly wound young first growth style wine may be more about symbolism than pleasure. In that case, choose something with a track record of approachability or some bottle age already in place.

If you are building a small cellar, buy with patience and variety. Not every bottle needs twenty years ahead of it. A smart mixed approach works better: some wines for near-term enjoyment, some with five to eight years of development, and a few with long horizons. That way, your collection remains useful rather than decorative.

For gifts, think about presentation and confidence. Magnum formats, vintage Champagne, classic Bordeaux and elegant Burgundy all carry occasion value. The trade-off is practicality. A magnum looks impressive but may be less convenient for a quiet household. A famous label impresses instantly but may cost more than an equally fine bottle from a less publicised estate.

Common mistakes this fine wine buying guide can help you avoid

Chasing scores without checking style is one of the most common errors. A highly rated wine may be superb yet still wrong for your palate or your event. Rich, powerful wines can dominate food. Delicate, mineral styles may disappoint someone expecting obvious weight.

Buying too young is another issue. Fine wines often need air, time or both. If you want something to open tonight, choose a bottle with maturity or a producer known for accessibility. Buying without checking bottle size can also catch people out. A standard 75cl bottle and a magnum create very different experiences, especially for parties and gifts.

Finally, do not ignore occasion pressure. Last-minute buyers often default to the most recognisable bottle in stock. Sometimes that is the right move. Sometimes a better result comes from choosing by style, region and readiness rather than by fame alone. A fast decision is still better when it is an informed one.

  • Pétrus: Nestled on the Right Bank in Pomerol, Pétrus is an exclusive producer crafting 100% Merlot wines in tiny quantities, approximately 3,000 cases annually. Consistently scoring 98–100 points from leading critics, these wines command secondary market prices ranging from £2,000 to over £5,000 per bottle, underscoring their rarity and desirability.

Demand, particularly from Asian collectors, has driven prices to unprecedented heights. The 2009 and 2010 vintages remain benchmark investments, revered for their power and impeccable aging potential.
  • Left Bank vs Right Bank: The Left Bank, comprising appellations like Médoc (including Margaux, Pauillac, and Saint-Julien), features Cabernet Sauvignon-dominant wines that are structured, tannic, and built for long-term aging. Conversely, the Right Bank, which includes Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, focuses on Merlot-dominant blends that are rounder and more approachable earlier but equally capable of aging gracefully.

Burgundy

Burgundy is famed for its complex terroirs and microclimatic variations, which are reflected in its celebrated climat vineyards. Its wines are prized for their finesse, depth, and capacity to reflect unique soil and microclimate nuances. Burgundian wines command record prices largely due to scarcity, producer reputation, and an insatiable global collector demand.

  • Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC): The apex of Burgundy investment wine, DRC is the world's most valuable wine estate. The Romanée-Conti Grand Cru produces fewer than 6,000 bottles annually, with auction prices regularly reaching £15,000 to £30,000 per bottle. Other DRC wines such as La Tâche, Richebourg, and Échézeaux are similarly coveted for their extraordinary investment value and rarity.
  • Domaine Leroy: Founded by Lalou Bize-Leroy, Domaine Leroy practices biodynamic viticulture and produces minuscule quantities. Musigny and Chambertin wines from Leroy represent some of the most sought-after Burgundies in the secondary market due to their purity, expression, and rarity.

En Primeur Buying Guide

En primeur, or "wine futures," is a system whereby Bordeaux châteaux release wines for sale approximately 18 months prior to bottling at prices typically below anticipated secondary market value. Buyers pay upfront and receive the wine 2 to 3 years later. This method offers access to coveted allocations of highly sought-after wines at release prices well before they become available on the secondary market.

Noteworthy en primeur campaigns include 2009, 2010, 2015, and 2016—widely considered some of the most successful modern-era investments, with buyers enjoying significant price appreciation. Though en primeur carries risk, as buyers must rely on the producer and merchant's reputation, provenance is firmly established from the moment of purchase.

Wine as a Wasting Asset - UK Tax Advantages

In the UK, wine is classified as a wasting asset under HMRC guidelines, meaning it is generally exempt from Capital Gains Tax (CGT) when sold at a profit. This makes fine wine one of the few investment classes with a built-in tax advantage for UK investors - a key reason why demand for investment-grade Bordeaux and Burgundy continues to grow. Unlike equities, property, or gold, fine wine held for personal enjoyment or investment purposes typically falls outside the CGT regime, making it an exceptionally tax-efficient alternative asset for UK collectors and investors.

Risks & Mitigation in Wine Investment

Investing in fine wine, while lucrative, involves several risks that require careful management to protect capital and maximize returns. Key risk factors and mitigation strategies include:

  • Market Volatility: Economic shifts, changing consumer preferences, and global events can cause fluctuations in wine prices. Staying informed on market trends and diversifying across regions and vintages can reduce exposure to sudden downturns.
  • Storage & Insurance: Proper storage in professional bonded warehouses is critical to maintaining wine quality and provenance. Bonded facilities provide tax advantages, consistent temperature and humidity control, and security. Adequate insurance coverage protects against physical damage or loss.
  • Fraud & Provenance: The fine wine market faces risks from counterfeit bottles and misrepresented provenance, which can severely impact investment value. Mitigation involves purchasing from reputable merchants, demanding full provenance documentation, and utilising trusted certification and authentication services.
  • Liquidity: Fine wine is a physical asset and not instantly liquid. Selling bottles can require time to locate buyers and complete transactions, particularly for rare or niche wines. Investors should plan for holding periods and consider liquidity needs when building a portfolio.

By understanding these risks and implementing recommended mitigation strategies, investors can safeguard their fine wine assets and capitalize on the market's long-term appreciation potential.

Condition & Provenance Assessment

When assessing investment wines, consider the following crucial elements:

  • Fill Level: High fill (within 1cm of the cork) is essential. Low fill indicates potential oxidation, depreciating value significantly.
  • Label Condition: Pristine original labels maintain value; damage or loss can reduce market value by 20–40%.
  • Cork Condition: Normal external mould is acceptable; however, corks pushed upward indicate heat damage and risk spoilage.
  • Storage History: Request detailed storage records. Wines stored temperature-controlled since release command notable premiums.

Frozen Cocktails: How to Make Them Taste of Something

The reputation of frozen cocktails is unfairly poor in Britain, largely because most of us have only encountered them as a luminous slush from a machine at a beach bar. Made properly, a blended drink is one of the genuinely great hot-weather formats: it cools you from the inside, it drinks slowly, and the texture does something no shaken drink can manage.

The reason most home attempts disappoint is not the recipe but the physics. Frozen cocktails are a different technical problem from stirred or shaken ones, and once you understand what changes, the results improve immediately.

Cold Hides Flavour, So Build the Drink Louder

Human taste perception drops sharply as temperature falls. Sweetness fades first, acidity follows, and aromatic compounds become far less volatile, which means less of them reach your nose. On top of that, blending introduces melted water, so the drink is diluted more than a shaken one and served at a temperature where you can taste it less.

The fix is to overbuild. Take a recipe you like and increase the sugar and the citrus by somewhere between a fifth and a third. Taste the unfrozen mixture before it goes in the blender: it should taste slightly too sweet and slightly too sharp at room temperature. If it tastes correct at that stage, it will taste of almost nothing once frozen.

Spirit strength matters too. Alcohol lowers the freezing point of the mixture, so a drink with more spirit will stay softer and scoopable, while a low-alcohol version freezes hard and separates. Around 20 to 25 per cent of the total liquid being spirit is a reasonable target for a blended drink that holds its texture.

Measure the Ice by Weight, Not by Handful

This single change transforms consistency. Use kitchen scales and start at 170 g of ice for every 100 ml of total liquid, then adjust for your own blender. Too little ice and you get a loose, soupy drink that separates into liquid and foam within two minutes. Too much and you get a stiff, pale mixture that labours the motor and tastes of cold water.

Blend on the highest setting you have, for around thirty seconds, and stop as soon as the sound changes from a rattle to a smooth hum. That change in noise is the most reliable signal that the ice has broken down evenly. Blending for longer simply melts what you have just made.

If your blender struggles, add the liquid first and the ice second so the blades have something to move through. Cheap jug blenders cope much better with smaller, thinner ice cubes than with large solid ones.

Four Builds Worth Making

A frozen daiquiri is the benchmark and the easiest to get right. Use 60 ml white rum, 30 ml lime juice and 20 ml sugar syrup with 190 g ice. The extra syrup relative to a shaken daiquiri is deliberate. White rum from the spirits range works better here than an aged one, since barrel character disappears almost entirely at these temperatures.

A frozen margarita wants 50 ml tequila, 25 ml lime, 20 ml orange liqueur and 10 ml agave syrup with 180 g ice. Salt the rim rather than salting the mixture, because a little salt at the lip does far more to sharpen the drink than salt dissolved through it.

A frozen wine slushie is the most underrated option for a garden. Blend 200 ml of a fruity red wine or rose with 150 g ice, 20 ml sugar syrup and a squeeze of lemon. It is closer to a sorbet than a cocktail and disappears alarmingly fast on a hot afternoon.

A frozen bitter spritz, made with 40 ml of an orange bitter aperitif, 60 ml prosecco poured in after blending, and 140 g ice, gives you the bitterness that most frozen drinks lack. Never blend anything sparkling, since the carbonation vanishes instantly and you will lose the pressure that makes it interesting. Fold it in at the end instead.

The Granita Method, and Why It Might Be Better

You do not need a blender at all. Mix the drink at roughly double its normal strength, since freezing dulls it further, and pour it into a shallow metal tray to a depth of no more than two centimetres. Metal conducts cold far better than plastic and will freeze it in half the time.

Every thirty minutes, drag a fork through the mixture to break the crystals apart. After two to three hours you have a coarse, spoonable ice with a crystalline texture that many people prefer to the smooth, homogenous result of a blender. It also holds up far longer in the glass, because the crystals melt individually rather than collapsing all at once.

This is the method to use for a party, since you can make it the day before and simply scrape portions out as needed.

Serving, Batching and Not Making a Mess

Chill the glasses. A frozen drink poured into a warm glass loses its texture in under a minute, and ten minutes in the freezer makes a visible difference. Coupes and small tumblers work better than large ones, because a frozen drink served in a big glass is warm sludge by the time anyone reaches the bottom.

For a group, blend in batches of no more than four servings, because overloading the jug produces uneven texture. Keep the finished drinks in a metal bowl inside a larger bowl of ice while you make the next batch, and stir the mixture once before pouring.

Finally, taste every batch. Ice varies, fruit varies, and the mixture that was perfect at four in the afternoon may need another squeeze of lime by seven.

The History of German Beer Day

German Beer Day is celebrated because of the creation of the Reinheitsgebot, the “purity law”, that was issued on the 23rd of April in 1516. 

The new law dictated how beer was brewed and sold in Bavaria, which permitted only water, barley and hops to be permitted in the beer. This law began to protect consumers from becoming victims to poor quality and overpriced beer.

The law gradually spread to the rest of Germany and was rolled out nationwide by 1906. The Reinheitsgebot is the oldest consumer protection law still in use but has seen several modifications over the years.

10 Popular German Beer Types to Try

Here we’ve listed 10 popular types of German beer for you to try this German Beer Day. 

Whether you’re looking to try something new or stick with a favourite, there’ll be a beer here for you. 

Lager

Lager, along with ale, is one of the two most common beer categories.

Lagers come in a variety of styles, which differ in colour, alcohol content and flavours.

Lager has an ABV of around 4-6%.

Weissbier

Weissbier is a classic Bavarian wheat ale that is top-fermented and known for its foamy and cloudy appearance.

Weissbiers are typically malty and have a subtle bitterness and are fermented with yeast strains that can typically provide clove, banana or smokey aromas.

Weissbier has an ABV of around 5%.

Pilsner

German Pilsner is a light, clean-tasting lager and is brewed from barley malt with spicy hop bitterness and a herbal, malty taste. Pilsner has an ABV of around 4 or 5%.

Bock

Bock beer is a strong German bottom-fermenting lager with an ABV of around 6.5%. Most bock beers have a mild bitterness and are slightly sticky from the malt sugars.

Altbier

Altbier falls somewhere between a lager and an ale - fermented warm like an ale but then aged cool like a lager.

Altbier is typically malty and crisp with a copper or amber colour. This beer has an ABV of around 4.8%.

Doppelbock

Doppel translates as double, so doppelbock is developed as a slightly stronger version of German bock style beer. Doppelbock has an ABV of around 7%.

Rauchbier

Rauchbier is translated as smoked beer, made with smoked malt. A clean and clear beer with medium hop bitterness, with smokey and malt tastes.

An easy-drinking beer with an ABV of around 3.9%.

Kölsch

Kölsch beer is a pale yellow, highly fermented, fully-rounded ale with an ABV of around 4.8%

Helles

Helles is a more malt-forward beer and has a firmer body than Pilsner and other lager styles. It is a clean, refined, dry, but fresh beer with light hop bitterness combined with subtle malt sweetness.

Helles has an ABV of around 5.5%.

Dunkel

Dunkel is a dark lager associated with Bavaria and Munich. This type of beer is typically smooth and subtly sweet with a subtle hop character- an easy-drinking beer.

Gin and Tonic Garnishes: Why the Lemon Slice Is Usually the Wrong Answer

The lemon slice became the default British gin and tonic garnish for entirely practical reasons. It was cheap, it kept behind the bar all evening, and in the era when almost every gin on the shelf tasted broadly similar, it did no harm. What it never did was make the drink better. Now that the shelf holds juniper bombs, citrus-led gins, floral gins and gins that taste of cardamom and black pepper, treating gin and tonic garnishes as one fixed habit throws away most of what you paid for.

The useful way to think about it is that garnish is an ingredient, not decoration. You smell a drink before you taste it, and a great deal of what you register as flavour is actually aroma arriving through the back of your nose. A garnish sitting at the surface of a tall, cold, fizzy drink is perfectly placed to dominate that first impression.

Start With the Gin, Not the Fruit Bowl

Every gin has a dominant character, and the garnish should either echo it or provide a deliberate counterweight. Read the bottle, taste the gin neat at room temperature first, and you will usually know within a sip which family it belongs to.

Juniper-led London Dry gins are piney, dry and slightly resinous. Grapefruit peel is the classic partner because its bitterness runs alongside juniper rather than fighting it, and the aroma is bright enough to stop the drink smelling austere. A single juniper berry, lightly crushed between your fingers, doubles down in a way that suits anyone who genuinely likes gin tasting of gin.

Citrus-forward gins, which lean on lemon peel, sweet orange and sometimes bergamot in the still, are the ones where a lemon slice does the least damage but still adds nothing. Orange peel is better. It picks up the sweeter end of the citrus and adds a rounder aroma that stops the drink reading as thin.

Floral and contemporary gins built around rose, elderflower, chamomile or cucumber need restraint. A wide strip of lime peel or three thin ribbons of cucumber gives lift without competing. Heavy citrus flattens them.

Spiced gins, and anything rested in a barrel, respond to warm aromatics. One green cardamom pod pressed open with the flat of a knife, five or six pink peppercorns, or a very short strip of orange peel with a single star anise will transform the drink. Go carefully, because cardamom and anise both take over quickly.

Peel Beats Slices, Almost Always

The aromatic oils in citrus live in the coloured outer layer of the skin. The flesh contains juice and acid, which are different things entirely. A slice of lemon dropped into a glass leaks juice into the drink, dulls the carbonation and pushes the whole thing towards lemonade. A strip of peel expressed over the surface delivers a burst of oil and almost no liquid.

Use a vegetable peeler rather than a knife and take a strip roughly four centimetres long, keeping as much white pith off the back as you can, since pith is bitter in the wrong way. Hold it skin side down about three centimetres above the glass and pinch it sharply. You should see a fine mist and smell it immediately. Then rub the strip around the rim and drop it in.

If you want the drink to look generous, a long spiral of peel wound around the inside of the glass does far more visually than a slice and adds only aroma. If you are pouring something from the gin and spirits range that you have not tried before, make the first one with peel alone so you can actually judge the gin.

Herbs, and How to Handle Them

Fresh herbs are the most underused category behind a home bar. Rosemary works beautifully with juniper-heavy gins, but only if you slap the sprig once against your palm to release the oils rather than bruising it to a pulp. A pulped sprig turns the drink medicinal within ten minutes.

Basil is excellent with citrus and floral gins, though it browns fast in ice, so add it at the last moment. Thyme is quieter than rosemary and better suited to lighter styles. Mint, despite its popularity, is usually a mistake in a gin and tonic. It is aggressive, it dominates every botanical in the glass and it belongs in drinks built around rum or spirits with more sugar behind them.

Whatever herb you use, one sprig is enough. Two makes a herbal tea.

The Garnish Only Works if the Rest of the Drink Does

No garnish rescues a warm, flat, over-diluted drink. Fill the glass properly with ice, right to the top, because a half-filled glass melts faster and dilutes more, not less. Use a copa or a highball rather than a tumbler, since the taller the drink and the wider the bowl, the more aroma collects where you can smell it.

Keep the tonic in the fridge, not just cool, and open it immediately before pouring. A 200 ml bottle per drink beats a large bottle that goes flat between rounds. Pour the tonic slowly down the side of the glass or over the back of a spoon to keep the bubbles alive, and stir once at most. Aggressive stirring is the fastest way to a lifeless gin and tonic.

Ratio matters too. Somewhere between one part gin to two parts tonic and one to three suits most gins, and stronger, more botanical gins can take the higher end without disappearing.

Combinations Worth Trying This Weekend

Grapefruit peel and a single juniper berry with a classic dry gin. Orange peel and a pink peppercorn with a citrus-led gin. Cucumber ribbon and a strip of lime peel with anything floral. Green cardamom and orange peel with a spiced gin. Rosemary and lemon peel together, with the peel expressed and the rosemary slapped, for a gin you find slightly too sweet.

What to avoid: dried fruit wheels, which look impressive and taste of nothing but stale sugar; frozen berries, which dilute into pink water; and the increasingly common habit of loading the glass with four different garnishes at once, which simply produces a fruit salad that happens to contain gin.

Building a Garnish Kit That Earns Its Keep

You do not need much. A lemon, a lime, an orange and a pink grapefruit will cover the overwhelming majority of gin and tonic garnishes, and they last a fortnight in a fridge drawer. Add a small pot of rosemary on the windowsill, a jar of green cardamom pods and a jar of pink peppercorns, and you can build a properly considered drink for any gin you happen to open.

Buy a decent peeler and keep it with the glasses rather than in a drawer full of knives, because the small friction of hunting for it is exactly what sends people back to hacking off a slice of lemon.

Short answer: It's about the exact vineyard the grapes come from, not the producer or the price alone. Grand Cru is a single, specific hillside in Chablis — about 100 hectares total, split into 7 named climats. Premier Cru covers a much larger area across roughly 40 different named vineyards, with real variation in quality between them. Both sit above standard "Chablis" and "Petit Chablis," which come from flatter, less favoured land.

The Actual Hierarchy, From Broadest to Narrowest

Chablis is unusual among French wine regions because it's made entirely from one grape — Chardonnay — so the classification system is purely about where the grapes grew, not what they're blended from. Four tiers, in ascending order of specificity and (generally) price:

  1. Petit Chablis — flatter, often north-facing plots at the edges of the region
  2. Chablis — the broad regional appellation, the largest volume tier
  3. Premier Cru (1er Cru) — around 40 named vineyards on better-exposed slopes
  4. Grand Cru — a single hillside of 7 named climats, all facing south-southwest across the Serein river from the town of Chablis

Why Grand Cru Is So Much Smaller Than Premier Cru

This is the part that surprises people: Grand Cru isn't just "the best of Premier Cru" — it's a genuinely tiny, specific piece of land. All seven Grand Cru climats (Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur, and Vaudésir) sit on one contiguous slope with ideal south-facing exposure and the region's purest Kimmeridgian limestone — the same fossil-rich soil, roughly 150 million years old, that defines Chablis's character. Because the aspect and soil are so consistent across this one hillside, Grand Cru wines tend to share a family resemblance: more concentration, more minerality, and real ageing potential.

Premier Cru, by contrast, is spread across many separate vineyards with real differences between them. A Premier Cru from Fourchaume (north-facing the Grand Cru slope, and considered one of the strongest Premier Cru sites) can taste meaningfully different from one grown in Vaillons, on the opposite side of town. This is why "Premier Cru" alone tells you less than "Grand Cru" — you also need to know which Premier Cru vineyard to know what you're actually getting.

Does Grand Cru Always Taste Better?

Not automatically, and this is worth being honest about. Grand Cru gives a wine more potential — better exposure, better soil, more concentration — but a mediocre producer can underperform their appellation, and a brilliant grower can make a Premier Cru that outclasses another producer's Grand Cru. The vineyard sets the ceiling; the winemaker still has to reach it.

That said, when comparing wines from the same producer, Grand Cru versus Premier Cru is usually a genuinely useful signal — most Chablis houses treat their Grand Cru parcels as their top wine and price and age them accordingly, often with more oak influence and longer ageing before release.

How to Taste the Difference

Premier Cru Chablis typically shows crisp green apple, citrus zest, and a clear chalky minerality — fresh, precise, food-friendly.

Grand Cru Chablis tends to layer in more richness alongside that minerality — riper orchard fruit, sometimes a honeyed or waxy texture from extended lees ageing, with real length on the finish. It's recognisably Chablis, just with more depth and structure.

Quick Reference

Premier Cru Grand Cru
Number of vineyards ~40 named climats 7 named climats, one hillside
Total area Larger, variable by site ~100 hectares total
Exposure Varies by vineyard Consistently south-southwest
Typical style Crisp, precise, mineral Richer, more concentrated, longer ageing potential
Price Above standard Chablis Above Premier Cru

History of Hennessy Cognac

Located in the Cognac region of France, the Hennessy cognac distillery was founded by Irishman Richard Hennessy in 1765, Irish officer serving in the army of Louis XV.

Following a record of productive growth in France and surrounding European countries, Hennessy was first imported to America in 1794, nearly 30 years after it was born.

The exportation to America signalled the birth of the cognac as an international that is celebrated to this day. That international recognition was first registered by The Prince of Wales, later King George IV of Great Britain. Being a great connoisseur of cognac, the King asked Hennessy in 1817 to create a “very superior old pale cognac” – and the Hennessy V.S.O.P was created. The initials V.S.O.P – Very Superior Old Pale – have been used since then as a standard for the entire cognac industry.

A year later, Empress Maria Federovna of Russia asked Maison Hennessy to produce his cognac as a birthday present for her son Czar Alexander, and that was how Hennessy found its way to cold Russia.

Having assumed the status of a global brand, the need came up forHennessy to have a widely recognized logo. The Cognac house deiced to go for an iconic fist clutching a hatchet as its official symbol in 1856. The symbol was used in memory of its founder Richard Hennessy’s 12-year career with the French army.

In 1865, Maurice Hennessy, great-grandson of founder Richard Hennessy, began to classify the brand based on stars. His use of varying numbers of stars to designate different quality, led to Hennessy’s Three Star Cognac, today known as V.S (Very Special). As with the V.S.O.P, this was copied by other brands in the industry.

Hennessy marked a significant feat in history when, in 1949, bottles of Hennessy 3-Star cognacs were packed as part of Paul-Emilie Victor luggage as he set out on his expedition to the Arctic. Right to say then that, Hennessy has journeyed from Cognac to the end of the world.

In the 1970s, Kilian Hennessy, assumed office as the CEO of Hennessy, and initiated the company’s 1971 merger with Moët et Chandon, which created Moët Hennessy. Moet Hennesy merged with Louis Vuitton in 1987, and the Louis Vuitton • Moët-Hennessy or LVMH was created – the world’sbiggest , luxury brand company.

What is Hennessy made from?

Like every other cognac, Hennessy is made from grapes grapes grown in the Charante region of France. With its chalky, stony soil and sunny temperate climate the region is perfect for vine growing.

For Hennessy, the cru is made up mostly of Ugni Blanc grapes, which have prevailed as the dominant grape in the Cognac region. Only the eau-de-vie from the first four crus is used due to its fruity, light white wine ideal for distillation.

The grapes are pressed to get the juice which is left to ferment for two or three weeks using modern fermentation processes, usually in October. Yeast is added to the juice, which helps convert the sugar in the juice into alcohol of about 7% to 8%.

The fermented juice is then distilled through a time-tested method which uses traditionally shaped Charentais copper stills, also known as an alembic. Two distillations must be carried out; the resulting eau-de-vie is a colourless spirit of about 70% alcohol.

The distillation process is done twice for the wine to qualify as a cognac – usually the resulting eau-de-vie is a white “water-of-life” spirit with 70% alcohol.

Once the distillation is done with, the wine is then stored in casks made from the nearby Limousin or Tronçais forest. The wood is perfect for aging cognacs due to their low resin content.

As the cognac interacts with the cask and air, it loses both alcohol and water – more of alcohol than water such that it reduces to 40%. The Cognac is then transferred to glass carboys called bonbonnes for storage before it is blended.

Throughout the aging period, the casks are sampled regularly by lowering a glass vial called a “prouvette” into an opening on the cask, according to a plan laid out by the Master Blender. The aging process sometimes lasts for centuries.

Blending of the cognac, or marriage, as it is otherwise called is necessary to achieve the unique taste peculiar to Hennessy. The Master Blender oversees the blending process to ensure that the mark of quality and taste remains consistent and true to the Hennessy standard.

The age of the cognac is calculated as that of the youngest component used in the blend. The blend is usually of different ages and from different local areas.

Once the blended cognac is ready, it is then bottled and your Hennessy cognac is ready. Hennessy was one of the first spirits brands to deliver its offerings in bottles.

The Origins of Don Julio Tequila

The Beginning of the Journey

Tequila is a drink that has become synonymous with Mexican culture and heritage. One brand that has played a significant role in shaping this legacy is Don Julio Tequila. Established in 1942 by Don Julio González, a visionary who saw the potential for a luxury tequila market, the brand has continued to flourish and evolve over the decades.

The Vision of Don Julio González

Don Julio González was a young man with a passion for tequila when he decided to create his own brand. He was determined to produce a tequila of exceptional quality, using only the finest ingredients and traditional production methods. Don Julio's commitment to quality and innovation would go on to transform the tequila industry.

The Distillation Process

Traditional Techniques

Don Julio Tequila is made using time-honored techniques that have been passed down through generations. The process begins with the harvesting of blue Weber agave plants, which are carefully tended for 7-10 years before they reach maturity. Once the agave has been harvested, the leaves are removed, and the piñas (the heart of the agave plant) are cooked in traditional masonry ovens to release their sweet juices.

The Importance of Agave Selection

A key factor in the exceptional taste of Don Julio Tequila is the careful selection of the agave plants. Only the highest-quality plants are used, ensuring that the tequila has a smooth, refined flavor that sets it apart from other brands.

Fermentation and Distillation

After cooking the piñas, their juices are extracted and fermented to create an agave must. This must is then double-distilled in copper pot stills to produce a clear, high-quality tequila. The tequila is then aged in American white oak barrels to develop its distinctive character and flavor profile.

The Evolution of Don Julio Tequila

The Introduction of Reposado and Añejo

As Don Julio Tequila grew in popularity, the brand expanded its offerings to include new varieties, such as Reposado and Añejo. Reposado tequila is aged for a minimum of two months but less than a year in oak barrels, giving it a mellow and complex flavor. Añejo, on the other hand, is aged for at least one year, resulting in a richer, deeper taste and a darker color.

Don Julio 70 – A Groundbreaking Innovation

In 2011, the brand celebrated its founder's 70th birthday with the release of Don Julio 70, the world's first Añejo Claro tequila. This innovative product combines the smoothness of a Blanco tequila with the complexity of an Añejo. The tequila is aged for 18 months in American white oak barrels and then carefully filtered, resulting in a crystal-clear spirit with a unique flavor profile.

Rather, like red wine, rosé almost always comes from red grapes, incorporating enough of their colour to make it pink, but not enough to qualify it as red wine.

The five methods of making rosé

The grapes’ skins, which impart flavour and tannins into the wine, may be left on or taken off at this point, depending on the type of wine being made, and the method used. The length of the fermentation period is also contingent on the kind of wine being made — more on how this relates to rosé later.

Overall, there are four main methods of making rosé: skin contact, pressing, run off and saignée, all of which carry out certain stages of the winemaking process slightly differently.

Let’s examine what each of these entails:

1. Skin contact

Also known as maceration, the skin contact method is the most popular way to make rosé. Just like red wine production, it involves crushing red grapes and leaving the juice in contact with the grapes’ skins.

However, unlike with red wine, the skins are only left to soak for a short amount of time so that the juice doesn’t turn too red. This can be for anywhere between six and 48 hours, in comparison to weeks or months for red wine.

Once the wine is the right colour, the juice is transferred into a tank for fermentation, minus the skins. This method can make a variety of types of rosé, depending on the duration of the maceration process.

2. Pressing

Similar to the skin contact method, pressing also keeps the grape juice in contact with the skins for a limited time. However, instead of allowing the juice to soak and gain colour, the grapes are immediately pressed to remove the skins, just like how white wine is made.

The red grape skin pigment means the juice will retain some colour (if only a small amount), which explains why this production method produces the lightest-hued rosé.

3. Run-off

The run-off method produces both rosé and red wine. In fact, the process began as a way to concentrate red wines, with the producer removing some juice during the maceration process.

This is then vinified separately as a rosé, while the remaining juice continues to vinify into a more concentrated red wine. The run-off method results in a darker rosé, which may not be to everyone’s taste.

4. Saignée

Saignée (also known as bleeding) arguably makes the best quality rosé, with rich and fruity varieties common.

This involves stacking up the grapes in a tank so that they get naturally crushed under their own weight, creating juice similar to the method of pressing rosé grapes.

Because the juice is only in contact with the grape skins for a limited period, the rosé produced through this method tends to be pale.

Short answer: In a refrigerator, chill champagne for 3 to 4 hours before serving. In an ice bucket (half ice, half water), it takes about 20 to 30 minutes. The right serving temperature is 8-10°C — cold enough to taste crisp and refreshing, not so cold that it mutes the aromas.

Why the Ice Bucket Method Is Faster Than a Fridge

An ice-and-water bucket cools a bottle roughly four times faster than a refrigerator alone. This is basic physics: water conducts cold far more efficiently than air, and the ice keeps that water at a constant 0°C throughout, rather than the fridge's fluctuating internal temperature. If you've forgotten to chill a bottle and a guest arrives in 25 minutes, the ice bucket is the only method that will actually get there in time.

To do it properly: fill a bucket or large container with equal parts ice and cold water, then submerge the bottle up to its neck. Give it a gentle turn every 5 minutes or so to keep the cooling even. Water alone, without ice, takes considerably longer — the ice is doing most of the work.

Why 8-10°C Is the Right Target, Not "As Cold As Possible"

Serving champagne too cold isn't a minor mistake — it actually mutes what you're paying for. Extreme cold numbs the palate and suppresses the delicate aromatics (brioche, citrus, orchard fruit) that distinguish a good champagne from a mediocre one. This matters more, not less, as the bottle gets more expensive: a straightforward non-vintage Brut can handle being served colder and still taste fine, but a nuanced vintage or prestige cuvée loses real character if it's served icy.

As a rough guide:

  • Non-vintage Brut, everyday drinking — 6-8°C is fine, slightly colder is forgiving
  • Vintage champagne or prestige cuvée — aim closer to 10-12°C to let the complexity show
  • Rosé champagne — similar to vintage, slightly warmer than you'd think, to bring out the red fruit character

What Happens If You Chill It Too Fast (Freezer Method)

Putting champagne in the freezer to speed things up is common, but risky. If you forget about it — which happens easily, since the difference between "chilled" and "frozen solid" is a matter of 20-30 minutes — the pressure inside the bottle combined with expanding, freezing liquid can crack the glass or force the cork out unexpectedly. If you do use the freezer as an emergency measure, set a timer for no more than 15 minutes and don't leave the room.

How Long Does Chilled Champagne Stay Cold Once Opened?

Once opened and out of the ice bucket, champagne warms up faster than most people expect — within about 20-30 minutes at room temperature, it's noticeably past its ideal serving window. If you're hosting, keep the bottle in the ice bucket between pours rather than leaving it on the table; this preserves both the temperature and the bubbles for longer.

How Much Ice for a Party: The Arithmetic Nobody Does

Ice is the only party supply that people consistently underestimate, and it is the only one that quietly destroys itself while you are not looking. Nobody runs out of glasses at nine o clock. Everyone runs out of ice.

The reason is that most of us think of ice as one thing when it is really two, with very different requirements. Working out how much ice for a party you actually need starts with separating those two jobs and doing some genuinely simple sums.

Chilling Ice and Serving Ice Are Different Purchases

Chilling ice sits in a tub or a bath with bottles and cans in it. Its job is thermal, it will get handled, splashed and rinsed by melting bottles, and nobody should be putting it in a glass. It can be the cheapest ice you can find, and the cubes can be any size or shape.

Serving ice goes in drinks. It should be clean, handled with a scoop rather than fingers, and stored separately from the moment it arrives. Ideally it is also in larger cubes, since a big cube has less surface area for its volume and melts more slowly in a glass.

Keeping them apart is the single most useful decision you will make. Most parties that run out of ice have not actually run out. They have contaminated their serving ice by using one tub for both, and by nine o clock nobody wants a cube that has been sitting under a beer bottle in murky water.

The Numbers That Actually Work

For a straightforward party where people are drinking from cans and bottles, allow 1 kg of ice per guest. That covers a tub for chilling and a modest amount for glasses.

For a cocktail party, or any outdoor party in warm weather, double it to 2 kg per guest. Cocktails are the reason. A shaken drink strained over fresh ice uses 200 to 250 g in total, because the shaking ice is thrown away. A long drink built in a highball uses around 150 g. Twenty guests having four drinks each works out at roughly 16 kg of serving ice on its own, before you have chilled a single bottle.

For chilling specifically, a rough guide is 500 g of ice for every four bottles or six cans you want to bring down to temperature within half an hour. If everything went into the fridge the night before, you can more or less halve that.

Melt Rate Is the Number Everyone Forgets

Ice does not sit patiently until needed. In a plastic tub in a warm room, expect to lose roughly a quarter of your ice every hour. Outdoors in direct August sun, it can be half. Over a five hour party, that means the ice you bought at midday is largely gone by the time the party properly starts, unless it has been insulated.

Insulation is worth more than volume here. A proper cool box with the lid closed will hold ice several times longer than an open plastic storage box, and a bin bag of ice wrapped in a blanket in a cold room outperforms both. Keep your reserve sealed and shaded, and only decant into the working tub as needed. Every time a lid comes off, warm air replaces cold.

Do not drain the meltwater from a chilling tub. Cold water is doing useful work, and draining it leaves the remaining ice sitting in warm air. The exception is if the tub is genuinely full and you need space for more bottles.

Your Freezer Is Not Going to Save You

A standard domestic freezer with trays produces somewhere around 1 to 2 kg of ice in twenty four hours, and each tray takes several hours to freeze solid. Making 10 kg would take most of a week of emptying and refilling trays, and it would fill the freezer you also need for food.

Treat home ice as a small reserve for the final hour rather than the main supply. If you do want to make some, fill the trays with cooled boiled water for slightly clearer cubes, and freeze them a couple of days early so they have time to harden fully. Ice that has only been in for three hours is soft and will vanish in a glass.

Silicone moulds that make 5 cm cubes are a worthwhile purchase if you serve spirits regularly. One large cube in a glass of whisky from the spirits range will outlast four small ones and dilute the drink far less.

Timing, Storage and the Practical Bits

Buy or arrange ice as late as you sensibly can. Ice bought at nine in the morning for an evening party has been melting for ten hours before anyone arrives. Mid-afternoon is the sweet spot for an evening event.

Store bags of ice flat rather than upright, since a flat bag has less surface area exposed and the cubes are less likely to fuse into a solid block. If they do fuse, drop the bag once on a hard floor before opening it rather than attacking it with a knife.

Have a scoop, a jug or a dedicated container for serving ice, and put it somewhere separate from the drinks tub so that guests naturally use the right one. A pair of tongs beside the glasses is a small thing that keeps the serving ice clean all evening.

Finally, buy more than the calculation suggests. Leftover ice costs almost nothing and goes back in the freezer, while running out at ten o clock means warm drinks for the rest of the night.

Gin Tasting at Home: How to Build a Flight That Teaches You Something

Most gin tastings go the same way. Someone lines up eight bottles on the kitchen island, everyone has a large one with tonic, and by bottle three nobody can tell the difference between any of them. A proper gin tasting at home is a smaller, slower, more deliberate exercise, and it is genuinely one of the most rewarding things you can do with a spirit. Gin is the most legible category on the shelf. Unlike whisky, where cask influence dominates, gin wears its recipe openly. You can smell juniper, coriander seed, angelica, orris root, citrus peel and whatever else the distiller has added, and with a bit of structure you can learn to name them within an evening.

Here is how to build a flight that actually works, whether you are doing it for two people on a Friday night or eight around a table.

Choose a theme before you choose bottles

The single biggest mistake is picking four gins you already like. They will almost certainly be four versions of the same idea, and the tasting turns into a coin-flip between near-identical London Drys. Instead, choose an axis of contrast and buy along it.

Three themes reliably deliver a good evening. The first is style contrast: one classic juniper-forward London Dry, one contemporary citrus-led gin, one floral or fruit-led modern gin, and one navy strength bottled at 57% ABV. The second is strength: the same broad style at 37.5%, 40%, 43% and 57%, which is startlingly educational because it shows how much of what people call flavour is actually texture and alcohol. The third is place: a Plymouth-style gin, a London Dry, a juniper-heavy continental gin and a Mediterranean-style bottle, showing how regional traditions shape a supposedly standard category.

For a first attempt, the style contrast flight is the one to run. It gives the widest spread of aroma and the clearest talking points. Browse the spirits range and pick one bottle from each camp rather than four from the same shelf.

Set the table properly

You need one glass per gin per person, which sounds like a lot until you realise the pours are tiny. Small tulip glasses or copitas are perfect; white wine glasses are a fine stand-in. Label them, either with a paper mat numbered one to four or a strip of masking tape on the stem. Numbering rather than naming matters if you want honest opinions, because brand recognition is a heavy thumb on the scale.

Alongside the glasses, put out a jug of room temperature still water, plain crackers or a bowl of bread, and a spittoon or empty jug for anyone who wants to spit rather than swallow. Nobody ever does at a home tasting, but offering it signals that this is a tasting rather than a session, which changes how people drink. Keep the room free of strong cooking smells and ask people to skip perfume, which sounds fussy until someone wearing a citrus scent sits next to you.

Pour in the right order

Work from lightest to heaviest, and from lowest to highest strength. A typical running order is: contemporary citrus gin, classic London Dry, floral or fruit-led gin, navy strength last. If you have a barrel-aged or Old Tom bottle, it goes at the end as well because sweetness and oak coat the palate.

Pour 15ml per person per gin. That is a third of a standard 45ml measure and plenty for three stages of assessment. Across six people that is 90ml per bottle, so a single 70cl bottle covers the evening comfortably with plenty left for cocktails afterwards.

Taste in three stages

Stage one is neat and dry. Nose the glass with your mouth slightly open rather than sniffing hard, because a hard sniff at 40% ABV just numbs you. Look for the pine and resin of juniper first, then peppery coriander, then the earthy sweetness of angelica and orris. Take the smallest possible sip and let it sit on the tongue.

Stage two is with water. Add three or four drops, no more, and re-nose. This is the moment people find surprising: citrus oils and floral notes that were buried behind alcohol come forward immediately. If a gin gets more interesting with water, it is usually well made.

Stage three is with tonic, at one part gin to three parts tonic, over plenty of ice, in identical glasses. Use the same tonic across all four, because switching tonics mid-flight makes the comparison meaningless. Garnish only after everyone has tried the drink unadorned, then experiment with a strip of grapefruit peel, a rosemary sprig or a slice of cucumber to see how much a garnish can pull a gin in one direction.

Take notes, and keep them simple

Hand out scraps of paper with three prompts: what does it smell like, how does it feel, would you buy it. Skip elaborate scoring systems. The goal is for people to commit to an opinion before the group discussion starts, because otherwise the loudest person in the room sets the consensus within thirty seconds.

Reveal the bottles at the end. There is nearly always at least one surprise, and it is usually that somebody has picked the cheapest bottle on the table as their favourite. That is a good outcome, not an embarrassing one.

What to serve alongside

Keep food neutral and let it come after the tasting rather than during. Salted crisps, plain crackers, hard cheese and cold cured meats all work. Fresh oysters and gin are a genuinely brilliant pairing if you want to be more ambitious. Have something else in the fridge for people who tap out early, whether that is a crisp white from the wine range or a few cold cans from the beer selection, and make sure there is still water within reach of everyone all evening.

Above all, keep it to an hour. Four gins, three stages, honest notes, bottles revealed, then move on to proper drinks. A gin tasting at home is at its best when it stays a curiosity rather than becoming a marathon.

A bottle marked vintage usually costs more, carries more prestige and gets more attention on the table. That is exactly why knowing how to buy vintage champagne matters. If you are buying for a dinner, a gift or a big date in the diary, the right bottle feels considered. The wrong one can be overpriced, poorly stored or simply not suited to the moment.

Vintage Champagne is not just ordinary Champagne with an older date on it. It is made from grapes harvested in a single year, and only released when a house believes that harvest was strong enough to stand on its own. Non-vintage Champagne is built for consistency. Vintage is built around character. That difference affects flavour, ageing potential, price and the kind of producer you should choose.

How to buy vintage champagne without overpaying

The fastest mistake buyers make is assuming older always means better. In Champagne, age, producer and storage all matter together. A 2008 from a top house that has been stored properly can be a superb buy. A random older bottle from a weak merchant with unclear storage history can be a risk, even if the year sounds impressive.

Start with the producer before the vintage. Well-known houses tend to have stronger quality control, consistent cellaring standards and clearer release histories. That makes buying easier if you want confidence rather than guesswork. If you know the house style you enjoy - richer and toasty, taut and mineral, or somewhere in between - you are already making a better decision than buying by year alone.

Price also needs context. Vintage Champagne should cost more than a non-vintage bottle from the same house, but there is a point where you are paying mainly for rarity or packaging rather than what is in the glass. If the occasion is a wedding gift, landmark birthday or client thank-you, that premium may be worthwhile. If you want the best drinking experience for the money, compare several respected houses instead of chasing the most famous label.

What makes a vintage worth buying

A good vintage is one thing. A good bottle to buy today is another. Some vintages are prized because they combine ripeness, freshness and longevity. Others can be charming young but less compelling later on. That is why blanket rules rarely help.

In practical terms, look for a vintage with a reputation for balance. Champagne needs acidity to age well. It also needs enough fruit concentration to avoid becoming thin over time. Buyers often focus on prestige years, but a less hyped vintage from a producer you trust can offer better value and earlier drinking pleasure.

Disgorgement matters too, even though many casual buyers overlook it. Champagne spends time ageing on the lees before disgorgement, and that shapes texture and complexity. Two bottles from the same declared vintage may drink differently depending on when they were disgorged and how long they have been ageing since. If that information is available, it can tell you whether the wine is likely to show more fresh tension or more developed biscuit and brioche notes.

How to read the label before you buy

If you want to know how to buy vintage champagne confidently, spend an extra minute on the label. The vintage year should be clearly stated on the front or back. If there is no year, it is not a vintage Champagne.

Then check the producer name, cuvee name and bottle size. Magnum can be especially attractive for vintage Champagne because larger formats often age more slowly and evenly. For gifting, though, a standard 75cl bottle is usually the easier and more practical choice.

You may also see terms like Blanc de Blancs or Blanc de Noirs. Blanc de Blancs is made from white grapes, typically Chardonnay, and often shows more citrus, chalk and tension. Blanc de Noirs is made from black grapes, usually Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, and can feel broader, richer and more powerful. Neither is automatically better. It depends on whether you want something precise and elegant or something fuller and more vinous.

Choose by occasion, not just prestige

The best bottle for an anniversary is not always the best bottle for a drinks reception. Vintage Champagne carries presence, but it should still fit the setting.
