Grower Champagne can offer something different. These producers make Champagne from their own vineyards and often show more individuality. Some are exceptional value, and they can be ideal if the recipient already enjoys wine and likes trying something less obvious.

The trade-off is familiarity. A grower bottle may impress a knowledgeable drinker, but it may not carry the same immediate recognition for a general gift recipient. If presentation and instant impact matter, a leading house still has an advantage.

Bottle size changes the decision

Standard 75cl bottles suit most purchases, but size can add practicality or theatre depending on the event. Magnums are particularly strong for parties because Champagne ages well in larger formats and they make an impression when carried to the table.

For gifting, large-format bottles also communicate generosity. They work especially well for milestone birthdays, engagements and corporate celebrations where a standard bottle might feel too modest. On the other hand, if the recipient is a couple or a single drinker, a standard bottle may be far more useful than a showpiece they will hesitate to open.

How to choose champagne for gifting

When the bottle is not for you, the smartest move is usually to reduce the risk. Choose a recognised house, stay with Brut unless you know they prefer something else, and think about whether the bottle should feel classic or luxurious.

If the recipient knows Champagne, you can be more specific. A vintage bottle, a Blanc de Blancs, or a prestige rosé can feel more considered than simply buying the biggest label. If you do not know their taste, avoid overcomplicating it. A premium non-vintage Brut in a presentation box is hard to get wrong.

Speed can matter here too. Last-minute gifting does not mean you have to settle for a poor bottle. A retailer with strong availability and clear category selection makes it much easier to send something that still feels intentional, especially when the occasion has arrived faster than expected.

A few mistakes worth avoiding

The most common mistake is buying on label prestige alone without thinking about who will drink it. A very dry, serious Champagne may impress on paper but disappoint guests who simply wanted something lively and approachable.

Another mistake is assuming rosé is only about appearance or that vintage is always better. Style matters more than status. The best bottle is the one that fits the moment.

Temperature is often overlooked too. Even excellent Champagne can seem flat or awkward if it is served too warm. Chill it properly, but do not freeze it into muteness either. You want lift, freshness and texture, not a bottle so cold it tastes of almost nothing.

If you are choosing in a hurry, keep it simple. Occasion first, then style, then budget. That framework will take you most of the way, whether you are planning ahead or ordering on demand.

Champagne should feel exciting, not stressful. Buy for the moment in front of you, trust the classic styles when you need a safe choice, and save the more specialised bottles for drinkers who will appreciate the detail.

You do not need to know every château in Bordeaux or every cru in Burgundy to buy well. If you have ever stood in front of a premium wine range wondering what actually makes one bottle worth £30 and another £300, this guide on how to choose fine wine is built for that moment - fast, practical, and clear enough to use when you are buying for tonight, for a gift, or for a proper celebration.

What fine wine really means

Fine wine is not just expensive wine. Price matters, but it is not the whole story. A fine wine usually comes from a respected region, a strong producer, a good vintage, or a combination of all three. It tends to offer more balance, complexity, ageing potential and a clearer sense of place than an everyday bottle.

That does not mean every fine wine must be old, rare or difficult to drink. Some are generous and ready to enjoy now. Others are built for cellaring. The key is knowing what you are buying it for, because the right bottle for a dinner party is not always the right bottle for an anniversary gift or a long-term investment purchase.

How to choose fine wine for the occasion

Start with the occasion before you start with the label. This saves time and usually leads to a better bottle.

If you are buying for drinking now, look for wines with approachability as well as pedigree. A well-made Barolo may be famous, but some examples need years to soften. A high-quality Rioja Reserva or mature Bordeaux can be easier to enjoy straight away. If the bottle is for a gift, recognisable regions and classic names often land better than something obscure, unless the recipient already knows exactly what they like.

For business gifting, you are usually safer with established regions such as Champagne, Bordeaux, Chablis or Napa Valley. They signal quality quickly. For a dinner party, matching the wine to the food and the crowd matters more than choosing the most prestigious label in the room.

Know the main styles before you buy

Most fine wine decisions become easier once you narrow the style. Think in terms of what the wine tastes like and how it will be used.

Fine white wine can range from crisp and mineral to rich and oak-aged. Chablis and top Sancerre are ideal when you want freshness, precision and food-friendliness. White Burgundy often brings more texture and depth. Riesling can be one of the smartest buys in fine wine, but it depends whether you want dry, off-dry or sweet.

Fine red wine covers an even wider spread. Pinot Noir tends to be lighter in body, fragrant and layered. Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux blends are firmer, more structured and often more age-worthy. Syrah can be savoury and peppery, while Nebbiolo offers perfume, tannin and seriousness. If you know the drinker prefers soft, plush reds, a young classified Bordeaux may not be the best fit just because it carries prestige.

Sparkling wine needs the same thinking. Vintage Champagne, grower Champagne and prestige cuvée all have their place, but not every celebration calls for the most expensive bottle. Sometimes a very good non-vintage Champagne from a respected house is the better buy, especially when you want consistency and immediate drinking pleasure.

Region matters, but producer matters more

A famous region helps, but it should not do all the work. Great producers in less fashionable appellations can outperform average producers in big-name regions.

When deciding how to choose fine wine, look at the producer as a quality signal. Houses and estates with a strong track record are more reliable across vintages. In regions with huge variation, such as Burgundy, producer reputation can be the difference between a remarkable bottle and an overpriced one.

This is especially useful if you are buying online and need to make a quick, confident decision. If the producer is known for consistency, the risk drops. If you are choosing between two similar wines at different prices, the stronger producer often justifies the premium more than the grander-sounding appellation.

Vintage is useful, not absolute

Vintage matters most in regions where weather conditions strongly affect quality. Bordeaux, Burgundy, Champagne and Barolo can all show significant vintage variation. That said, a great producer in a difficult vintage can still make a better wine than a weak producer in a celebrated year.

If the wine is for immediate drinking, do not chase vintage headlines alone. A blockbuster year can produce wines that are powerful but still tight and youthful. A slightly softer vintage may actually drink better now. If the bottle is intended for ageing or collecting, then vintage becomes more important because structure, concentration and longevity move up the priority list.

Price should tell you something - but not everything

There is a point in fine wine where you stop paying only for quality and start paying for rarity, status and demand. Sometimes that is worth it. Sometimes it is not.

At entry fine wine level, spending a bit more often does buy a clear step up in depth and craftsmanship. Move further up, and the gains become narrower. A £60 bottle may dramatically outperform a £20 one. The jump from £150 to £300 can be much smaller unless you care about collectability, scarcity or prestige branding.

That is not a reason to avoid expensive wine. It is a reason to buy with purpose. If the goal is to impress a knowledgeable recipient, provenance and label recognition may matter. If the goal is a brilliant bottle for supper, value can come from lesser-known estates, mature vintages from overlooked years, or strong regions sitting just outside the spotlight.

Consider age and drinking window

One of the biggest mistakes in fine wine is assuming older always means better. Some wines improve with age. Others lose their freshness and charm if left too long. Many fine wines sold today are ready to drink, but some still need time.

Check whether the wine is built for early enjoyment or development. Mature wines can be superb for gifting or special dinners because they offer complexity without the wait. Younger wines may be more vibrant but less settled. If you need the bottle for this weekend, it is worth choosing a wine with a drinking window that starts now rather than in five years.

Fine wine for gifting

A gift bottle has to do two jobs at once. It should feel premium on arrival, and it should be enjoyable when opened.

Recognition helps. Champagne, classified Bordeaux, Barolo and grand cru Burgundy all carry weight, but they suit different recipients and budgets. Presentation matters too. Gift sets, large-format bottles and vintage-dated wines can make more impact than chasing the highest critic score.

If you are sending wine as a last-minute present, convenience should not force a compromise on quality. Avoid these common buying mistakes

The first is buying on region name alone. Prestige can mask an average producer or an awkward vintage. The second is ignoring the drinker. A serious bottle that does not suit their taste is still the wrong bottle.

The third is treating critic scores as the final answer. Scores can be useful, but they do not tell you whether the wine is elegant or bold, mature or youthful, generous or austere. The fourth is overbuying tannic or age-worthy wines for immediate drinking. Fine wine should suit the moment, not just the label.

A quick way to narrow your options

If you want a practical shortcut, make your choice in this order: occasion, style, region, producer, vintage, then price. That sequence keeps the decision grounded in what you actually need.

For example, if you need a polished red for a client dinner tonight, you might land on a mature Bordeaux from a reliable château rather than a young Barolo with bigger reputation but less immediate appeal. If you need a luxury gift, a vintage Champagne or a large-format bottle may be the smarter move because the impact is obvious the moment it arrives.

How to choose fine wine with more confidence

Confidence does not come from memorising every grape and vintage chart. It comes from recognising a few dependable signals and using them quickly. Think about the drinker, the occasion, whether the bottle is for now or later, and whether the producer has earned the price.

Fine wine should feel exciting, not like an exam. The smartest bottle is usually the one that fits the moment perfectly, arrives when you need it, and tastes every bit as good as it looks when the cork comes out.

How to Keep Drinks Cold at a BBQ Without Losing Half Your Ice by Noon

Every British barbecue follows the same arc. Someone tips two bags of ice into a cool box at eleven in the morning, everybody admires it, and by two in the afternoon it is a lukewarm paddling pool with three sad cans floating in it. The problem is almost never the amount of ice. It is how the ice is being used. Working out how to keep drinks cold at a BBQ is less about buying more and more about understanding that ice does its job in water, not in air, and that a drink already at room temperature is a drink you are paying for twice.

What follows is the practical version, built around how heat actually moves, with the numbers you need to plan properly rather than guess.

Water Beats Air Every Single Time

The single biggest improvement you can make costs nothing. Fill your tub or cool box with ice, then add cold water until the drinks are properly submerged. It feels wrong, as though you are melting your own ice on purpose, but water conducts heat away from a can roughly twenty five times faster than air does. A can sitting in a nest of ice cubes only touches cold in a handful of places. The same can in an ice slurry is touching cold everywhere at once.

In practice this is the difference between a lager being drinkable in twelve minutes and being drinkable in an hour. It also means you can chill in batches rather than trying to keep forty cans cold all afternoon, which is the real cause of most ice failures. Keep the bulk of your stock in the shade in its boxes and rotate a dozen drinks through the ice bath at a time.

The Salt Trick, and Why It Is Not a Myth

Add a good handful of ordinary table salt or rock salt to your ice bath, stir it through, and the water will drop several degrees below zero without freezing solid. Salt lowers the freezing point of water, so the ice is forced to keep melting and each gram of melting ice pulls a large amount of heat out of whatever is sitting in the bath.

A salted bath will get a bottle of white wine from cupboard temperature to serving temperature in around fifteen minutes instead of twenty five. The trade off is that your ice disappears faster, so treat the salted bath as a rescue tool for drinks you need cold urgently rather than the default for the whole day. Use roughly 250 g of salt to a large tub, and never use that meltwater for drinking ice.

Pre-Chilling Is the Step Everyone Skips

Cooling a drink is a fixed amount of work. If you hand your ice a crate of 21 degree beer, it has to do all of that work in the garden, in the sun, in the middle of your party. If the beer went into the fridge the night before, the ice only has to hold it steady, which it can do for hours on the same quantity.

The night before, get as much as will fit into the fridge. On the morning, put the overflow into the freezer for no more than forty five minutes with a timer set, because forgotten cans burst and forgotten sparkling wine can push its cork. Anything that will not fit anywhere should at least be kept indoors and out of direct sun. Cardboard cases left on a patio can reach well above air temperature, and glass holds that heat stubbornly.

Building a Tub That Survives the Whole Afternoon

Insulation is worth more than volume. A cheap plastic storage box loses cold through every wall, whereas a proper cool box or even a tub wrapped in a couple of old towels and a picnic blanket will hold ice several times longer. Put it in shade, keep the lid on, and resist the urge to drain the meltwater. Cold water is still cold, and draining it leaves your remaining ice sitting in warm air.

Two containers work better than one large one. Run a working tub that guests dig into, and a reserve tub that stays closed and shaded, topping up the working tub as it thins out. Every time a lid comes off, warm air replaces cold, so a reserve that is opened twice an hour will outlast a single tub opened forty times.

If you have no ice at all, a wet tea towel wrapped around a bottle in a breeze will drop it several degrees through evaporation within twenty minutes. It is a genuine field technique, not a party trick, and it works best on a dry, moving day.

Getting the Temperature Right, Not Just Low

Cold is not automatically better. Very low temperatures suppress aroma and mute bitterness, which is why an ice cold lager tastes clean and refreshing while an ice cold stout tastes of very little. Serve crisp lagers such as Asahi, Peroni or Corona from the beer selection at 3 to 5 degrees, and let Guinness and richer ales come up towards 8 to 10.

The same applies to wine. Whites and roses want 8 to 10 degrees, not the 4 degrees a domestic fridge delivers, so take the bottle out fifteen minutes before pouring. Prosecco and champagne belong at 6 to 8 degrees, cold enough to keep the mousse fine without numbing the fruit. Lighter reds from the red wine range are genuinely improved by twenty minutes in the ice bath on a hot day. British room temperature in August is not the room temperature those wines were written about.

Spirits, Mixers and the Dilution Problem

Spirits do not need ice bath treatment, but their mixers absolutely do. A warm tonic ruins a gin and tonic faster than a warm gin does, because the mixer makes up most of the glass and warm liquid holds far less dissolved carbon dioxide. Keep tonic, soda and cola as cold as anything else you are serving, and chill your glasses if you have the freezer space.

Use large cubes rather than small ones for spirits served long. A big cube has less surface area for its volume, so it melts slower and dilutes less, which matters when a drink is going to sit in someone hand for half an hour in the sun. If you are pouring from the spirits range, that one change does more for the drink than any amount of garnish.

When the Ice Runs Out Mid-Afternoon

It always does, usually at the point when nobody wants to leave. Plan for a top up rather than a heroic morning shop: ice bought at nine in the morning has been melting for five hours by the time you need it most, so a mid-afternoon delivery of ice, mixers and another case of beer is simply better logistics.

Rum punch is a Caribbean concoction that adds a tropical twist to fruit punch recipes. Traditionally an assortment of fruit juices, punch originally came to the UK from India, before Jamaican rum was added to the drink further down the line.

Its name derives from the Sanskrit word for “five”, which is a nod towards the five key ingredients that usually make up this cocktail — alcohol, sugar, lemon, water, and tea or spices.

Some ingredients, such as the fruit juice, can be switched to suit your tastes, although you can’t go wrong with traditional rum punch. The native fruits found in these cocktails, like orange and pineapple, provide a natural sweetness that is the ideal match for most types of rum.

These Caribbean cocktail recipes perfectly combine sweet and sour flavours to create fantastic weekend drinks. Follow our selection of recipes and learn how to make rum punch by transporting yourself to a paradise beach in the tropics. And if you don’t have liquor in your drinks cabinet, don’t worry, as we can deliver it to your doorstep in just 30 minutes.

Rum punch recipes

How to make traditional rum punch

This sweet orange rum punch recipe makes enough for two glasses and allows you to choose whichever type of rum you fancy.

Ingredients

  • 175ml orange juice
  • 150ml rum (either light or dark—we’ve used light in this recipe)
  • 75ml lime juice
  • 50ml sugar syrup
  • Dash of grenadine syrup
  • Dash of Angostura syrup
  • Ice cubes, for serving
  • Generous pinch of freshly grated nutmeg
  • 2 thick slices of orange, for garnish
  • Maraschino cherries, to garnish

Method

  1. Pour the orange and lime juice, white rum, sugar syrup, grenadine and Angostura into a large jug and give it a stir
  2. Chill in the fridge for one hour
  3. Serve over ice cubes, sprinkle the nutmeg and garnish with an orange slice and Maraschino cherry (speared with a cocktail stick)

How to make Jamaican rum punch

This Jamaican rum punch recipe is a little different as the main ingredient is pineapple juice, making it a tropical favourite. It’s quick and easy to make, and all you need is a few minutes to concoct this cool drink. Remember not to skimp on the lime juice as it adds a zesty twist and packs a punch.

Makes one pitcher

Ingredients

  • 400ml pineapple juice
  • 400ml orange juice
  • 300ml dark rum
  • 50ml lime juice
  • 45ml grenadine syrup
  • Ice cubes, to serve
  • Citrus slices, to garnish
  • Maraschino cherries to garnish

Method

  1. Combine the pineapple, lime and orange juice, as well as the dark rum, and stir well
  2. Prepare the cocktail glasses by pouring one tablespoon of grenadine syrup into each glass and add the ice cubes
  3. Pop the citrus slices and Maraschino cherries onto cocktail sticks, ready for garnishing
  4. Pour the rum mix into the glasses — and don’t forget the garnish

How to make Bacardi rum punch

This Bacardi rum punch is perfect for any party, with its delicious mix of fruity juices. Bring a taste of the Caribbean to your party with this simple recipe, which makes enough for one large punch bowl.

Ingredients

  • 25ml Bacardi Carta Blanca rum
  • 25ml orange juice
  • 25ml pineapple juice
  • 10ml cranberry juice
  • 10ml Bacardi Carta Negra rum
  • 5ml grenadine
  • 1 lemon, sliced

Method

  1. In a large container, mix all of the liquid ingredients and place in the fridge until chilled
  2. Once refrigerated, pour into a large punch bowl with ice
  3. Garnish the bowl with floating lemon slices

If you are working out how to order party drinks, the real question is not just what people like to drink. It is how much to buy, how to cover different tastes, and how to get everything in place without turning the host into a last-minute stock manager. Order too little and the evening stalls. Order too much and you are left with random bottles nobody wanted in the first place.

The smartest approach is to treat drinks like any other part of the event plan. Start with the guest list, match the drinks to the occasion, and build in enough flexibility for the way people actually drink rather than the way you hope they will. A birthday flat gathering, a garden party, a corporate event and a dinner party all need a different drinks plan.

How to order party drinks for the kind of event you are hosting

Before you think about brands or bottle counts, get clear on the format of the party. A short evening drinks gathering usually needs a different mix from an all-day celebration. If people are arriving after work for two or three hours, wine, beer, soft drinks and one easy spirit option often cover it. If you are hosting from afternoon into late evening, consumption naturally stretches, and your order needs more depth.

Food matters just as much. If you are serving a full meal, guests usually drink more steadily. If it is mostly nibbles, crisps and canapes, sparkling wine, beer and lighter mixed drinks tend to move faster. For richer food, red wine and fuller white wines make sense. For lighter menus, Prosecco, rosé, Sauvignon Blanc and gin-based serves are often easier wins.

The guest mix changes everything too. A party for close friends can be ordered quite tightly because you already know what people lean towards. A broader crowd needs more range. If you have colleagues, partners, family and neighbours all in one room, do not overcommit to one style. Variety is what keeps the bar area moving smoothly.

Start with headcount, then work backwards

One of the easiest mistakes when deciding how to order party drinks is buying by instinct. Headcount is the starting point, but it needs context. Fifty guests at a three-hour engagement drinks reception are not the same as fifty guests at a house party that runs until midnight.

As a rough planning rule, think in drinks per person rather than bottles first. For a shorter event, many guests will have two to four drinks. For a longer one, that number can move higher, especially at weekends and celebration-led occasions. Not everybody drinks alcohol, and not everybody drinks the same amount, so averages are useful only when paired with a sensible mix.

Then turn that into categories. If your crowd is mixed, wine is often the foundation because it works across a range of tastes. Beer gives easy coverage. Sparkling wine adds a celebration cue. Spirits should be chosen selectively rather than trying to stock a full back bar at home. One or two spirit bases are usually enough unless you are hosting something larger with a dedicated drinks station.

Soft drinks and water should never be an afterthought. They are what make the whole order feel complete. Guests will alternate, designated drivers will need proper options, and mixers disappear quickly when people are making simple serves.

Build a balanced drinks order

The most effective party order is balanced rather than ambitious. That means you are not trying to please every possible preference with ten categories. You are covering the obvious choices well.

For many parties, a dependable mix looks like sparkling wine for arrival drinks or toasts, white and red wine for general drinking, beer and cider for casual reach, and one or two spirits with matching mixers. If the event feels more premium, Champagne can replace standard sparkling wine, and the wine selection can be tightened around stronger labels or regions rather than broadened.

There is also a practical question of speed. Guests naturally gravitate towards drinks they recognise and can serve quickly. A fridge full of beer, a chilled white wine, a crowd-pleasing rosé and a good bottle of gin with tonic often outperform a more complicated spread of niche liqueurs and half-matched mixers.

If you know your crowd prefers spirits, choose a lane. Gin and tonic is easy. Vodka with soda, tonic or cola is straightforward. Whisky works better for smaller groups or later-evening occasions where people will sip rather than mix heavily. Rum can be brilliant for a more relaxed party, but only if you know guests will actually drink it.

Don’t guess quantities by bottle alone

This is where hosts either waste money or get caught short. Bottles look reassuring when they arrive, but quantity planning works better when you think in serves.

A standard bottle of wine gives around six medium glasses. A bottle of Champagne or sparkling wine gives roughly the same, though for toasts the pours are often smaller. Spirits go much further, but only if you have enough mixers, ice and garnish to support them. Beer and cider are simpler because each bottle or can is effectively one serve.

If your event is wine-led, you can plan the core around white, red and sparkling and then add beer as a secondary choice. If it is more casual, beer and cider may do more of the heavy lifting, with wine supporting. For summer parties, chilled rosé and sparkling often move faster than expected. In colder months, red wine and darker spirits can see a stronger share.

The best safeguard is a modest buffer, not a huge surplus. A little extra in your most popular categories makes sense. Buying a large volume of fringe options does not. Extra tonic, soda, cola, still water and sparkling water usually saves more parties than an extra obscure spirit ever will.

Match the drinks to the time of year and tone

Seasonality is not just a nice detail. It changes what people reach for.

In warmer weather, crisp whites, rosé, Prosecco, Champagne, lager, cider and long spirit serves are the obvious winners. Guests want cold, refreshing options and they tend to drink them faster. That means chilling space matters as much as the actual order.

In autumn and winter, richer reds, fuller-bodied whites and darker spirits feel more natural. Sparkling wine still works well for celebrations, but beer and cider choices may shift slightly depending on the crowd. If the event is smart, go cleaner and more classic. If it is casual, keep it easy and generous.

Tone matters too. A birthday with music and open-house energy calls for broad appeal and easy serving. An anniversary dinner needs less volume and better bottle quality. A corporate gathering benefits from a more polished selection with strong non-alcoholic coverage. Guests read the room through the drinks almost immediately.

When to order party drinks

Timing is part of how to order party drinks properly. Leave it too late and you are forced into whatever is available. Order too early and you can end up storing more than your space allows, especially if you need everything chilled.

For planned events, place the order once the guest count is reasonably stable and the menu is set. That gives you enough certainty to buy with confidence. For spontaneous occasions, speed and availability matter more than perfect optimisation. In that scenario, it helps to choose categories that solve the problem quickly rather than overthinking every bottle.

If you are hosting in London and realise on the day that your numbers have increased, a fast alcohol delivery service can be the difference between a smooth event and a mid-party scramble. That is exactly where Drinks House 247 fits best - immediate top-ups, strong selection and the ability to cover both straightforward party staples and more premium celebration bottles.

Common mistakes that cost hosts money

The biggest mistake is overbuying spirits and underbuying basics. A party can survive with one fewer premium bottle on display. It struggles if there is no tonic, no ice, or not enough white wine chilled.

Another common issue is buying for your own taste. If you love peaty whisky or natural orange wine, that does not mean the room does. Personal favourites are fine as part of the mix, but they should not dominate the order unless the guest list genuinely supports it.

Hosts also underestimate soft drinks. Good hosting means everyone is looked after, not just the people drinking alcohol. Premium soft drinks, adult alternatives, juices and plenty of water make the party feel better organised and more generous.

Finally, avoid making the drinks offer too complicated. The more decision points you create, the slower service becomes. Keep the range clear, chill what needs chilling, and make sure the most popular options are easiest to reach.

A better way to think about the order

The best party drinks order is not the biggest one. It is the one that fits the occasion, the guest list and the way people actually drink. Enough choice to keep everyone happy, enough quantity to carry the event, and enough quality that the drinks feel considered rather than rushed.

If you get those three things right, the drinks stop being a hosting worry and start doing what they should do - keeping the atmosphere easy, the glasses full and the evening moving.

Decanting wine

Decanting wine is simply the process of adding air to your wine, which helps to enhance the aromas, giving you the best experience when drinking. The easiest way to do this is to pour the wine from its bottle into a jug. You can get special decanters which are specifically designed for use with wine, and are traditionally bowl-shaped, with a long, tapered neck for pouring.

When decanting wine, you should pour it slowly into the decanter. Any sediment that may be at the bottom of the bottle will then stay there, giving you a clear wine to enjoy. Pouring your wine slowly also increases the amount of oxygen it comes into contact with, opening up its flavours and aromas as much as possible.

Some people choose to double decant, which simply means pouring the wine back into the (rinsed) bottle, or into another decanter. This adds even more oxygen to the wine, getting the aromas out even more fully. Try this if you find that your wine needs something extra after a single decant.

You may also choose to let your wine breathe. This helps to open up the bouquet, letting you take in the aromas before the first sip, which works to enhance the drinking experience. To do this, simply decant your wine a few hours before you plan on drinking it.

Temperature

While we’ve already mentioned that you should avoid serving red wine too chilled, there are some preferred temperatures to serve wine.

Lighter, white wines, such as Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc, and Chablis, should be served at around 10°C. Full-bodied whites, such as oaked Chardonnay and Vognier, can be served at a slightly warmer temperature, up to 15°C.

Medium-bodied red wines, like Pinot Noir and Grenache, should be served at a maximum temperature of 16°C, while full-bodied reds should be drunk anywhere between 16-19°C. Merlot, Syrah, and Cabernet Sauvignon are examples of these warmer red wines.

All of these wines can be served by themselves or with a delicious cheese platter - perfect for sharing with dinner guests!

How to store wine

Any wine should be stored in a cool, dry, dark area of your home. Excessive exposure to light, or fluctuating temperatures, can actually alter the taste of the wine in your bottle, causing it to go bad over a prolonged period of time. Any moisture in the air can even seep into the cork, which may end up mixing with the wine, and damage it over time.

If your bottle is sealed with a cork, you should store the bottles horizontally. This keeps the cork moist, which is crucial to its longevity, as dry corks are susceptible to crumbling, potentially causing the wine to leak out. It also introduces air to the wine, which ages it and can cause it to go bad before you’ve had a chance to drink it.

When it comes to storing open bottles of wine, you should try and recork it whenever possible. You can do this by wrapping the cork in wax paper, which will help it slide back into the neck of the bottle more easily. However, as this isn’t always appropriate — if the cork has split, for example — it’s a good idea to invest in a wine stopper to keep the bottle sealed.

When you do open a bottle of wine, we recommend drinking it within a week, even if you have managed to recork or seal the open bottle.

If you have ever stared at a wine list, a gift page or a shop category and thought, just show me the style I actually like, shopping wine by grape variety is the fastest way through the noise. It cuts past unfamiliar labels and regions and gets you closer to the flavour in the bottle, whether you are ordering for dinner tonight, sending a gift, or replacing a bottle you enjoyed before.

For most buyers, grape variety is more useful than appellation jargon. You may not remember every village in Burgundy or every sub-region in Rioja, but you will remember that you like Sauvignon Blanc when you want something crisp, or Malbec when you want something rich and easy to pour with steak. That is why grape-led browsing works so well for modern wine buying - it is practical, quick and far easier to repeat.

Why shop wine by grape variety?

Regions matter, but grape often gives you the clearest first signal. If you know the variety, you can usually predict the body, acidity, fruit profile and general mood of the wine with reasonable accuracy. That is valuable when you are buying in a hurry or choosing a bottle for someone else.

It also helps when the same grape appears in different countries. A Chardonnay from Chablis, South Africa or California will not taste identical, but the variety still gives you a useful starting point. You can then refine by country, producer, price or style depending on how specific you want to be.

There is a trade-off, though. Some wines are blends, and some of the world’s best bottles are known more by region than by grape. If you only shop by variety, you can miss part of the picture. The smart approach is to use grape as the shortcut, then use region and producer as the fine tuning.

The main wine grapes worth knowing

You do not need to memorise dozens. A small set of popular varieties covers most buying decisions and makes choosing much faster.

White wine grapes

Sauvignon Blanc is the clean, sharp option people often reach for when they want freshness. Expect citrus, gooseberry, green apple and herb notes, especially in cooler styles. It works well for seafood, goat’s cheese and lighter starters, but it is also a reliable bottle for informal drinks when you want something lively.

Chardonnay is broader and more flexible. Unoaked Chardonnay can be fresh and mineral, while oaked styles bring vanilla, butter and a rounder texture. That range is exactly why some people say they dislike Chardonnay when in fact they only dislike one style of it. If you are buying for a mixed group, Chardonnay is often a safe middle ground.

Pinot Grigio is light, straightforward and easy to serve. It tends to be dry, crisp and uncomplicated, which is part of its appeal. If the occasion is casual and the brief is simply a chilled white that most people will enjoy, Pinot Grigio does the job.

Riesling deserves more attention than it usually gets. It can be bone dry or gently off-dry, and the acidity keeps it focused either way. Good Riesling is excellent with spicy food, and it is one of the best examples of why checking the producer and style matters just as much as the grape itself.

Red wine grapes

Cabernet Sauvignon is structured, dark-fruited and often full-bodied. Think blackcurrant, cedar and firm tannins. It suits roast beef, hard cheeses and more formal dinners, but it is also a strong gifting choice when you want a red with classic appeal.

Merlot is softer and plusher. It usually brings ripe plum, black cherry and a smoother finish, making it approachable for a wide range of drinkers. If someone says they want a red that is not too heavy and not too sharp, Merlot is often the answer.

Pinot Noir is lighter in body but not in character. Expect red cherry, raspberry, spice and earthy notes depending on where it is from. It can feel more delicate than Cabernet or Malbec, which makes it an excellent choice with duck, mushroom dishes and meals where a powerful red would dominate.

Malbec has become a go-to for rich, fruit-forward red wine. It is generous, dark and easy to enjoy, especially with grilled meat. For buyers who want impact without too much complexity, Malbec is one of the simplest wins.

Shiraz, sometimes labelled Syrah, brings body, spice and dark fruit. In cooler expressions it can be peppery and savoury; in warmer climates it becomes fuller and more opulent. It is a strong option for barbecues, hearty food and bold-flavoured menus.

Wine by grape variety is not always the whole story

A grape tells you a lot, but where it is grown changes the result. Climate, winemaking and ageing all shape the final style. Sauvignon Blanc from the Loire can be flinty and restrained, while New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc is often louder, greener and more tropical. Both are Sauvignon Blanc. They just answer different moods.

That matters when you are restocking a favourite. If you loved a silky Pinot Noir from Burgundy, a cheaper Pinot from a warmer region may taste jammier and less refined. Equally, if you want value and immediacy, that brighter, fruit-led version may be exactly right. It depends whether you are buying for a Tuesday night dinner, a client gift or a special celebration.

Blends add another layer. Bordeaux reds are often led by Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, while many Southern Rhône wines combine Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre. In those cases, shopping by grape can still help, but you are really shopping by the balance between grapes rather than one single variety.

How to choose quickly without getting it wrong

Start with the drinker, not the label. Ask what they usually enjoy. If they order crisp whites in restaurants, look at Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio or dry Riesling. If they like smooth, generous reds, go towards Merlot or Malbec. If they talk about elegance, Pinot Noir is a better fit than something heavily oaked or highly tannic.

Then think about the occasion. A weekday bottle needs less ceremony than an anniversary gift. For parties, consistency matters more than nuance, so crowd-pleasing grapes often beat niche choices. For gifting, recognised varieties and premium producers make life easier because the recipient instantly understands the style and quality cue.

Food is the final check. High-acid whites sharpen seafood and salads. Fuller reds carry roast meats and richer sauces. Spicy dishes usually need freshness or a little softness, not aggressive tannin. You do not need textbook pairings, just enough awareness to avoid clashes.

A practical way to browse wine by grape variety online

Online shopping works best when categories are clear. Browsing by grape variety helps you narrow a large range quickly, especially when you already know the style you want. From there, you can filter by country, price point, brand or occasion.

That is particularly useful for fast ordering. If you need a last-minute bottle for guests, or a next-day gift with a more premium feel, variety-led browsing reduces the time spent second-guessing labels you do not know. On a site like Drinks House 247, where the range spans everyday bottles through to fine wine and celebration gifting, that structure makes the shop easier to use and the decision easier to trust.

Which grapes are best for gifting?

If you are buying for someone whose taste you do not know well, stick with grapes that are familiar and broadly liked. Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Malbec, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon are usually safer than highly aromatic or very niche varieties. Recognition matters in gifting because the bottle has to feel both useful and premium.

If the recipient is more wine-savvy, you can be more precise. A fine Pinot Noir, a well-made Riesling or a top Chardonnay can feel more thoughtful than simply defaulting to the biggest name. The best gift is not always the most famous grape. It is the one that suits the person and the occasion.

When to move beyond grape variety

Once you know your preferences, the next step is to layer in region and producer. If you like Chardonnay, ask whether you prefer lean and mineral or rich and oaked. If you enjoy Cabernet Sauvignon, decide whether you want classic structure or ripe New World fruit. This is where wine buying becomes less random and more rewarding.

Still, grape variety remains the quickest entry point. It is how many people build confidence, repeat successful purchases and avoid wasting money on bottles that miss the mark. You do not need to speak fluent wine to buy well. You just need a reliable way in.

The easiest bottle to choose is usually the one that starts with a grape you already trust, then matches the moment you are buying for.

Drinks Trolley Ideas That Work Beyond the First Fortnight

A drinks trolley is one of the few pieces of furniture that is simultaneously decorative and useful, which is why it keeps coming back into fashion. It is also the piece most likely to end up as an expensive shelf holding four bottles nobody drinks, a dusty cocktail shaker and a novelty gin someone gave you in 2019.

The difference between a trolley that gets used and one that becomes ornamental comes down to what you put on it. These drinks trolley ideas are built around actual use rather than photography, though a well-stocked trolley happens to look better than a badly stocked one anyway.

The six bottles that do the work

Every classic cocktail worth making comes from a small number of base spirits. Stock these six and you have covered the ground:

A London Dry gin for Martinis, Negronis, gin and tonics and a French 75. A vodka, which you will use more than you expect for guests who do not like anything else. A bourbon or rye for Old Fashioneds, Manhattans and Whiskey Sours, with rye giving a drier, spicier result. A white rum for Daiquiris and Mojitos. A blanco tequila for Margaritas and Palomas. And a brandy or cognac, the most neglected bottle on most trolleys, for Sidecars and for pouring after dinner when nobody wants another cocktail.

Everything else is optional. Browse the spirits range and buy the six before you buy a seventh flavour of anything.

The modifiers matter more than the seventh spirit

The thing that separates a trolley that makes good drinks from one that makes crude ones is not more base spirits. It is modifiers.

Sweet vermouth and dry vermouth unlock the Negroni, the Manhattan and the Martini, three of the most requested drinks in the world. Orange liqueur such as triple sec or Cointreau unlocks the Margarita, the Sidecar and the Cosmopolitan. Angostura bitters goes into more classic recipes than any other ingredient and a bottle lasts for years. Add Campari if you like bitter drinks and maraschino liqueur if you get serious.

Make a simple sugar syrup by dissolving equal parts caster sugar in hot water, keep it in a bottle in the fridge, and it lasts a month. That single step improves every sour, every Daiquiri and every Old Fashioned you will ever make at home.

What should not live on the trolley

Three things. First, cream liqueurs, which need refrigeration after opening and will separate if left warm. Second, anything already open and delicate, meaning vermouth, sherry, port and most aperitifs. They are fortified wines and they oxidise. Keep them in the fridge and bring them out when you make the drink; a bottle of vermouth left open on a warm trolley for six weeks is the reason so many people think they dislike Martinis.

Third, wine that you actually care about. A trolley is warm, light and vibrated every time someone walks past. Store wine somewhere cool and dark and keep only one or two display bottles on the trolley itself, whether from the wine range or a bottle of fizz that is destined for opening soon.

Glassware and kit, kept honest

You need fewer tools than any cocktail book suggests. A jigger with 25ml and 50ml measures, a Boston shaker or a cobbler shaker, a mixing glass, a bar spoon, a Hawthorne strainer, a fine mesh strainer and a decent peeler. That is a complete kit and it fits on one shelf.

For glassware, four rocks glasses, four coupes and four highballs will handle every drink above. Coupes are more useful than martini glasses because they hold their contents when someone gestures with them. If space is tight, skip the highballs and use the rocks glasses for everything short.

Add a small cutting board, a paring knife and a bowl for citrus. Fresh lemons and limes are not optional. Bottled juice is the single biggest difference between a home cocktail and a bar one, and not in your favour.

Arranging it so it actually works

Use the top shelf for what you use most: the six spirits, standing at the back, with the working surface at the front kept clear so you have room to build a drink. Bottles at the back, space at the front, not the other way around.

Use the lower shelf for glassware, tools, and anything heavy. Weight at the bottom stops the trolley tipping when it is wheeled, which matters if it has small castors and your floors are uneven.

Group by colour and height rather than by category if you care how it looks. Tall clear bottles behind, short dark ones in front. A single plant, a stack of small napkins or a low bowl of citrus breaks up the glass and stops it looking like a shop display.

Keeping it good

Wipe the bottles down every few weeks, because sticky necks and dust are what make a trolley look neglected. Rotate anything that is nearly finished to the front so it gets used rather than lingering at half an inch for a year.

Keep ice in mind. A trolley cannot store ice, so keep a decent silicone mould in the freezer and make large cubes the night before you plan to host. Large cubes dilute at roughly half the rate of small ones, which is the difference between an Old Fashioned that holds up and one that turns watery.

Finally, keep a few mixers and something cold in reserve. A trolley is for spirits; the fridge does the rest. A few cans from the beer selection and a bottle of champagne or prosecco covers the guests who do not want a cocktail at all.

We can all agree that hangovers are no fun. With a constant headache, tiredness, and feeling sick, it’s no wonder that we use the common phrase ‘I’m never drinking again’. 

Whilst the obvious solution is to never drink again, most of us don’t want to give up our social drinking habits or our favourite tipple forever. 

So, knowing how to stop a hangover, could be the difference between enjoying your night out and feeling alright in the morning, compared with regretting the night before. 

Drinks House 247 have put together some top tips on how to stop a hangover, so you can wake up feeling fresh.

Before Drinking

Eat Fatty & High-Fibre Foods 

It’s always good to ‘line the stomach’ before drinking alcohol, and it’s recommended that you eat fatty and high-fibre foods. This is because they’ll delay the body’s absorption of alcohol. 

Easy foods to eat would be avocado, lentils and popcorn as they break down the alcohol and absorb it, keeping it from reaching the bloodstream as quickly. 

Load Up on Vitamin C

Vitamin C can help fight colds, but it can also guard against hangover symptoms. Try making a fresh fruit smoothie and stock up on oranges and watermelon. 

Avoid Sugar

Sugar can cause inflammation, and so can alcohol. So, it’s no good hunting down a sugary treat to have before going out.

Whilst Drinking

Choose Your Drinks Carefully

It's recommended to avoid congeners, which are compounds that give liquor its flavour and colour. Most alcohol contains them, however, darker alcohols, like red wine and whiskey, generally have a lot more. Congeners are chemicals that can set off inflammatory responses that bring on hangover symptoms. 

As well as this, it's better to avoid anything too bubbly, such as champagne or prosecco. This is because it can speed up the rate of alcohol absorption and the stomach can expand due to the carbonation. 

This is why it’s a good idea to stick to one kind of drink throughout the evening, such a lighter spirits like vodka and gin. It’ll also mean you can keep track of how much you’re drinking. 

Pace Yourself

Just because you’re drinking the same type of alcohol, doesn’t mean you can drink quicker. It’s a good idea to pace yourself throughout the night and if you really want to avoid a hangover, limit yourself to no more than one drink per hour. 

Alternate with Water

Sticking to one drink and pacing yourself are two good steps to take, but to go one step further, you can alternate your alcoholic drink with a glass of water. This will not only replenish your hydration levels, but also keep the hangover at bay. 

After Drinking

After getting home after your night out, there are a few simple steps you can take to avoid that dreaded hangover in the morning. 

Have a Pint of Water Before Bed

Drinking a pint of water before going to sleep will hopefully save you from waking up with a dry mouth. It may also help with detoxification processes overnight. 

Eat Before You Sleep

As well as drinking water, eating some food before going to bed could theoretically help slow the alcohol absorption and stabilise blood sugar.

Get a Good Night’s Sleep

It's important that you get a good night's sleep, as not getting enough sleep could make your hangover worse. 

Alcohol disrupts your sleep, and you could sleep lighter than usual, which is why you may find yourself waking up early when the sun rises. We recommend popping a sleeping mask on to minimise environmental disruptions.

Short answer: Most champagne is non-vintage (NV) — a blend of grapes from multiple years, made to taste the same every time. A champagne is only vintage if the label states a specific year, such as "2013" or "2015." No year on the label means it's non-vintage, regardless of how the bottle looks or how much it costs.

How to Check a Specific Bottle

Look at the front label. If you see a four-digit year printed there, it's vintage — that bottle was made entirely from grapes harvested in that single year. If there's no year, or the label says "NV" explicitly, it's non-vintage.

A few examples to make this concrete:

  • Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label — no year on the label. Non-vintage.
  • Dom Pérignon — always shows a year (e.g. 2013). Dom Pérignon is made only as vintage champagne; the house doesn't produce a non-vintage line at all.
  • Laurent-Perrier Cuvée Rosé — no year. Non-vintage.
  • Louis Roederer Cristal — always shows a year. Vintage only.

Some champagne houses make both. Moët & Chandon's Brut Impérial is non-vintage, while their Grand Vintage line carries a year. If you're comparing two bottles from the same producer, checking for a year is the fastest way to tell them apart.

Why This Isn't Just Trivia

Vintage and non-vintage aren't just labels — they're made differently, on purpose:

Non-vintage champagne is a deliberate blend of reserve wines from several harvests, sometimes going back many years. The winemaker's job is consistency: a bottle of Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label should taste essentially the same whether you buy it this year or in five years. This is the house's signature style, engineered to repeat.

Vintage champagne is only made in years the house considers good enough to bottle alone. Many producers skip vintage releases entirely in mediocre years — some declare a vintage only three or four times a decade. By law, vintage champagne must age on its lees for a minimum of three years before release (compared to 15 months for non-vintage), and premium houses often age it far longer.

Does One Taste Better Than the Other?

Not automatically — they're built for different things. Non-vintage is designed to be reliably good and repeatable, which makes it the right choice for most everyday drinking and gifting. Vintage is designed to express something specific about one growing season — it can be more distinctive, more age-worthy, and more expensive, but "better" depends on whether you want consistency or character.

There is a particular kind of Saturday morning that arrives before every August bank holiday. Why the Bank Holiday Weekend Catches Everyone Out

Two things happen at once. First, London empties and refills unpredictably, so shops stock to a forecast that is frequently wrong. Second, everyone decides to host on the same two days, and they decide late, because nobody commits to an outdoor plan in Britain until the forecast is more or less settled.

The result is that supermarket shelves thin out in a specific order rather than uniformly. Nobody runs out of everything. They run out of the obvious things, and the obvious things are precisely what you were planning to buy.

What Actually Runs Out First

In rough order: ice, then chilled lager in multipacks, then prosecco, then chilled rose, then mixers, then decent tonic. Notice how many of those are chilled rather than ambient. Shops can have plenty of stock in the back and still have nothing cold on the shelf by Sunday lunchtime, which is no use at all if you are serving in two hours.

Spirits are the exception. Gin, vodka, whisky and rum rarely sell out, because people buy a bottle rather than a case and the turnover is slower. If your plan depends on something being cold, though, assume you will need to chill it yourself.

If you have no time to think, this covers a mixed gathering of around fifteen people across an afternoon and evening. Two cases of lager, with something crisp like Peroni, Asahi or Corona doing the heavy lifting and a few Guinness or Stella for the people who want something with more body. Chilling Under Time Pressure

This is where most last-minute hosting goes wrong. A domestic fridge packed with warm cans takes two to three hours to bring them properly cold, and it will chill nothing else in the meantime.

The reliable fix is an ice bath: ice, cold water and a good handful of salt in a bucket or a clean washing-up bowl. Water conducts heat far better than air, so full contact with the bottle does in twelve minutes what a fridge does in two hours. Keep the bath topped up through the day and use it as your serving station rather than shuttling bottles back and forth.

Buy more ice than feels sensible. A rough guide is one kilo per person for a warm afternoon, and that is before you factor in anything you are chilling rather than serving.

Order Once, Properly, Then Top Up

The temptation with last minute bank holiday drinks is to under-order on the grounds that you can always nip out. On a bank holiday Monday in London, nipping out is exactly what several thousand other people are also doing, and the shop nearest you will have been stripped since Sunday.

A better approach is to order the bulk of it the day before, chill overnight, and treat any mid-party shortfall as a delivery rather than an expedition. Worth checking our delivery areas in advance so you are not finding out mid-party.

Weather changes what people drink more than any other factor. A hot, still bank holiday shifts consumption heavily towards cold beer, cider and soft drinks, and away from red wine and spirits almost entirely. A grey, cool one does the reverse: the red wine disappears and people move indoors and settle in.

If the forecast is genuinely uncertain, weight your order towards beer and white wine, which are useful in either scenario, and hold back on the reds and the heavier spirits until you can see what Monday looks like. It is far easier to add than to be left with a case of something nobody touched.

London Dry Gin vs Old Tom and Plymouth: What the Names Actually Mean

Gin labelling is unusually confusing because the three most historically significant terms on the shelf describe three completely different kinds of thing. One is a production rule, one is a place, and one is a style with no legal definition at all. Understanding the London dry gin vs Old Tom distinction, and where Plymouth fits between them, does more for your drinking than memorising any number of brand names.

Here is what each term means, what it tastes like, and which drinks were actually written with it in mind.

London Dry Is a Method, Not a Postcode

London Dry is a legally defined production standard, and geography has nothing to do with it. To carry the name, a gin must take all of its flavour from botanicals distilled together with the spirit. Nothing may be added after distillation except water and a very small permitted quantity of sweetening, and no colouring is allowed at all.

That rule has a real consequence for taste. Because nothing can be added at the end, the distiller has to get everything right in the still, and the result is generally dry, precise and juniper-forward, with citrus and coriander seed doing much of the supporting work. There is nowhere to hide a mistake and nothing to smooth over a rough edge.

This is the style that most people picture when they think of gin, and it is the correct default for the drinks that define the category. A Dry Martini, a Negroni and a classic gin and tonic were all built around this kind of spirit. If you are choosing from the gin and spirits range and want one bottle that does everything, this is the style to buy.

Plymouth Is a Place, and It Tastes Like a Softer London Dry

Plymouth gin has been made continuously in the city since the late eighteenth century, and for many years the name carried a formal geographical protection. In practice it now denotes gin made at the single historic distillery in Plymouth rather than a broad category.

Stylistically it sits very close to London Dry but with the corners rounded off. There is less aggressive juniper, more earthy root character, and a slightly fuller, softer mouthfeel that comes from the botanical balance rather than from any added sugar. It is drier than Old Tom and softer than a typical London Dry.

Where it excels is in drinks where a very assertive gin fights the other ingredients. It makes a superb Dry Martini for anyone who finds a classic London Dry version too austere, and it is excellent in a gin and tonic with a grapefruit or orange peel garnish. Historically it was the specified gin in a great many pre-Prohibition recipes, so if an old cocktail book calls for Plymouth by name, it is worth taking seriously.

Old Tom Is the Missing Link

Old Tom is the style that connects Dutch genever to modern dry gin. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, distillation was cruder and the base spirit was rougher, so sugar was added to make gin palatable. As column distillation improved through the nineteenth century, the sugar became unnecessary, dry styles took over and Old Tom nearly disappeared.

It came back because bartenders rediscovered the classic cocktail repertoire and found that a great many recipes simply do not work with a dry gin. Old Tom is sweeter and fuller than London Dry, with a softer juniper profile and often a richer, more malty texture. There is no legal definition, so producers interpret it differently. Some sweeten a dry gin, some use a heavier distillate, and a few age it briefly in barrel.

The drinks that need it are specific. A Martinez, the ancestor of the Martini, is unbalanced and thin with London Dry. A Tom Collins was named for the style. A Ramos Gin Fizz benefits enormously from the extra body. In each case the sweetness is structural rather than decorative.

How to Substitute Without Ruining the Drink

You can move between the three, as long as you compensate for sugar and intensity.

Replacing Old Tom with London Dry means adding roughly 5 ml of sugar syrup per 50 ml measure, and accepting that you will not recover the body, only the sweetness. Going the other way, if a recipe written for London Dry is made with Old Tom, cut the syrup in the recipe by the same amount or remove it entirely.

Plymouth can replace London Dry in almost any drink with no adjustment. The result is gentler and slightly earthier, which suits stirred drinks better than shaken ones. Replacing Plymouth with London Dry works too, but consider using slightly less vermouth in a Martini, since the gin is doing more of the talking.

The one substitution that rarely works is using Old Tom in a Negroni or a Dry Martini. Both drinks depend on the gin providing dryness against sweeter ingredients, and Old Tom removes that tension.

Which One Should You Actually Buy?

If you own one gin, make it a good London Dry. It covers the entire modern repertoire, it works with tonic, and it is the reference point against which everything else is judged.

If you own two, add Plymouth. It gives you a genuinely different Martini and a softer gin and tonic without duplicating what you already have.

Old Tom is the third bottle, and it earns its place only if you make classic cocktails. Bought speculatively it tends to sit unopened, since it is not an ideal gin and tonic base. Bought because you want to make a proper Martinez, it is indispensable.

Taste all three side by side at room temperature before you mix anything with them. The differences are obvious neat and become subtle once tonic is involved, so the neat tasting is where you actually learn what you have bought.

A Malbec Wine Guide for People Who Want to Buy Better

Malbec has become one of the most reliable purchases on any wine shelf, which is exactly the problem. It is so consistently pleasant that most people stop paying attention and buy whichever bottle has a nice label. That is a shame, because the range within Malbec is enormous. A bottle from a high-altitude vineyard in the Uco Valley and a bottle from Cahors in south west France share a grape variety and almost nothing else.

This Malbec wine guide covers the things that genuinely change what is in the glass, so you can pick deliberately rather than hopefully.

The grape and its improbable second life

Malbec is French. It was one of the six permitted grapes of Bordeaux and the dominant variety of Cahors, where it made famously inky wine known as the black wine of Cahors. It is also thin-skinned, prone to frost, and susceptible to a fungal disease called coulure that ruins fruit set. The catastrophic frost of 1956 killed off most of what remained in Bordeaux, and growers largely replanted with Merlot instead.

Cuttings had reached Argentina in the mid-nineteenth century, and there the variety found a climate that suited it perfectly: dry, sunny, high, with meltwater irrigation from the Andes and almost no fungal pressure. Argentine Malbec today is not a copy of the French original. It is arguably a different wine made from the same plant.

Altitude is the single most useful thing on the label

If you learn one thing about buying Malbec, make it this. Mendoza vineyards range from around 600 metres above sea level up to 1,500 metres and beyond. Every hundred metres of elevation lowers the average temperature, increases the day to night temperature swing, and intensifies ultraviolet exposure.

The result is that lower altitude Malbec, from areas such as the eastern Mendoza plains, tends to be soft, jammy, high in alcohol and quick to drink. Higher altitude Malbec, from the Uco Valley or Gualtallary at 1,200 metres and above, keeps far more acidity, develops thicker skins and therefore more structured tannin, and shows floral violet aromatics, a chalky mineral edge and darker, less sugary fruit.

Many producers now print the altitude on the back label. If it says 1,000 metres or more, you are buying a fresher, more structured wine. If it says nothing, look for the sub-region: Uco Valley, Tupungato, Gualtallary and Altamira all indicate height.

Reading the rest of the label

Alcohol is your other quick indicator. A Malbec at 13.5 percent is likely to be fresher and more food-friendly than one at 15 percent, which will be riper, sweeter-seeming and heavier.

Oak matters enormously in this variety. Malbec takes oak readily, which is why so many cheaper examples taste of vanilla, coconut and coffee more than of grape. Terms such as roble or barrica indicate some barrel time. Wines labelled unoaked or made in concrete or amphora are increasingly common and show the fruit far more purely. If you have decided you dislike Malbec, there is a reasonable chance you actually dislike heavily oaked Malbec.

Vintage matters less than for European reds, since Mendoza is a desert with irrigation and enjoys reliable weather, but 2016 was famously wet and difficult, so avoid it unless the producer is very good.

Cahors and the savoury alternative

If you find Argentine Malbec too soft or too sweet-tasting, Cahors is the answer, and it is one of the best value red wines in France. Legally at least seventy percent Malbec, usually blended with a little Merlot or Tannat, Cahors is grown on limestone plateaus and river terraces in a cooler, wetter climate.

The wines are dark, dense and distinctly savoury, with black plum, iron, graphite, dried herbs and firm tannin. They need food and they reward five to ten years of ageing, which very few Argentine Malbecs do. A good Cahors alongside a slow-cooked casserole is one of the more satisfying pairings in wine.

Serving it properly

Serve Malbec at 16 to 18 degrees. Served too warm, and most British homes do serve red too warm, the alcohol becomes prominent and the fruit turns stewed. Twenty minutes in the fridge before opening fixes it.

Decant young Malbec for thirty to forty five minutes. It genuinely opens up, and the violet and floral notes that distinguish good examples only really appear after air. Use a glass with a decent bowl rather than a small tumbler.

Most Malbec is made to drink within three to five years of the vintage. A small number of top single-vineyard wines from Uco will improve for a decade or more, but there is no need to lay down a mid-priced bottle.

What to eat with it

Steak, obviously, and specifically something with fat and char. Ribeye over sirloin. Beyond that, lamb chops with rosemary, slow-cooked beef short rib, chorizo, empanadas, aubergine cooked over charcoal, mushroom risotto and hard sheep cheeses all work. Chimichurri, with its parsley, garlic, oregano and vinegar, is close to a perfect partner for the herbal edge in a high-altitude Malbec.

What does not work is delicate white fish, subtle chicken dishes and hot chilli. Alcohol amplifies capsaicin heat, so a 14.5 percent Malbec with a fiery curry makes both worse.

Choosing a bottle

For a weeknight, take a mid-priced Uco Valley Malbec with modest oak. For a barbecue or a steak night, something riper and richer from classic Mendoza. For a proper dinner where you want the wine to be interesting, a Cahors or a single-vineyard Argentine bottle at 1,200 metres. Look through the red wine collection or the wider wine range, and if you are hosting, a couple of bottles alongside something from the beer selection covers most guests comfortably.

Ordering a case of wine sounds simple until you realise how much can hide behind the word mixed. One retailer means a smart six-bottle spread across regions. Another means leftover stock bundled under a tidy label. This mixed wine cases review is for buyers who want the convenience of a pre-built selection without ending up with three bottles they would never choose twice.

For most people, a mixed case is not about building a cellar. It is about solving a need quickly and well. That might mean sending a polished gift, stocking up for a dinner, covering different tastes for a weekend gathering, or trying new styles without committing to a full case of one label. The right case saves time. The wrong one creates clutter in the rack and regret at checkout.

Mixed wine cases review - what actually makes a good case?

A strong mixed case should feel curated, not assembled. That sounds obvious, but it is the key difference between a useful buy and a forgettable one. You want a sense that each bottle has earned its place, whether the case is built around grape variety, country, price point or occasion.

Balance matters first. A six-bottle case with five sharp Sauvignon Blancs and one heavy red is not really mixed in a meaningful way. A better selection gives you contrast in body, acidity and style. That could mean a crisp white, a richer white, a light red, a fuller red, something fruit-led and easy, and one bottle with a bit more structure. The exact blend depends on the goal, but variety should be deliberate.

Quality consistency matters just as much. One excellent bottle cannot carry five average ones. In practice, a good mixed case usually avoids wild swings in standard. You may get one standout bottle and a few everyday drinkers, but the whole set should sit within a sensible quality band.

Then there is drinkability. Some cases look impressive on paper but are awkward in real life. If every wine needs decanting, cellar temperature and a long meal, that is not convenient for most buyers. Good mixed cases include bottles you can open on a Tuesday and bottles you can pour when guests arrive on Saturday.

When a mixed wine case is better than buying bottles individually

If you already know exactly what you like, bottle-by-bottle shopping can make more sense. But mixed cases work well when speed matters, or when you are buying for more than your own palate.

They are especially useful for gifting. A single bottle can feel too narrow unless you know the recipient well. A mixed case gives breadth and looks more considered. It also suits corporate gifting and thank-you occasions where you want quality without overcomplicating the choice.

They also help when hosting. Few groups all want the same thing. Some guests will go straight for a clean white, others prefer a softer red, and someone always wants something a bit more interesting than the safe option. A properly assembled mixed case covers the room without forcing you to browse dozens of individual listings.

There is also value in trial. If you are trying to move beyond your usual supermarket favourites, a mixed case can introduce new regions and grapes with less risk. You are not betting on twelve bottles of something unfamiliar. You are spreading that risk across a selection.

What to look for in a mixed wine cases review before you buy

The first thing to check is whether the case has a clear theme. It does not have to be narrow, but it should make sense. “Summer whites”, “classic Europe”, “easy-drinking reds” and “dinner party favourites” are all useful concepts. “Best sellers” can also work, but only if the wines genuinely represent broad appeal rather than stock-clearing.

Next, look at the producer mix. Cases that lean on known regions and reliable producers tend to perform better than those padded with anonymous labels. You do not need every bottle to come from a famous estate, but recognisable winemaking intent matters. A Rioja should taste like Rioja for a reason, not just because the label says so.

Price transparency is another signal. If the retailer claims a large saving, it should still be possible to judge the wines on their own merit. Deep discounts can be genuine, but they can also distract from a weak selection. A fair mixed case often wins on convenience and sensible curation rather than dramatic headline savings.

Bottle sequence is worth thinking about too. In a good case, you can imagine a natural order of drinking. Lighter wines first, richer ones later, perhaps one bottle that feels a little more premium. That progression suggests someone has thought through the customer experience.

The trade-off between variety and coherence

This is where mixed cases often go wrong. Some try too hard to be broad, which leaves the selection scattered. Others become so tightly themed that they stop being versatile.

A case built around six different countries may sound exciting, but if the styles clash and quality is uneven, it can feel random. On the other hand, six bottles from one region may be excellent, yet not much use if you want flexibility across a few occasions.

The best middle ground depends on why you are buying. For home drinking, a little more experimentation is welcome. For gifting, coherence usually matters more. For a party, drinkability should lead. For a client gift or celebration order, presentation and bottle recognition often carry more weight.

This is why there is no single best mixed wine case, only the best fit for the job.

Best types of mixed wine cases for different buyers

If you are buying for casual drinking, look for cases built around approachable styles and broad food compatibility. Think fresh whites, smooth reds and bottles that do not demand too much explanation. These cases should be easy to open and easy to enjoy.

If you are buying as a gift, premium cues matter more. Region, producer reputation, smart presentation and a sense of occasion all count. In that setting, a mixed case with a clear identity usually lands better than one chasing maximum variety.

If you are buying for a dinner or gathering, balance across styles is key. You want a case that can move from aperitif to main course without leaving gaps. A split between whites and reds is the obvious starting point, but texture matters too. One aromatic white, one mineral white, one softer red and one fuller red often goes further than simply choosing by colour.

If you are buying in a hurry, convenience becomes part of value. A well-organised retailer with clear category pages, useful product detail and dependable fulfilment can save more frustration than any small price difference. That matters even more if the case is part of a gift or a last-minute event shop. Drinks House 247 is built around that exact buying behaviour, especially when timing matters as much as the wine itself.

Red flags that usually mean skip it

Be wary of vague descriptions. If a case tells you almost nothing about grape, region, style or producer, there is a reason. Good wine retail does not hide the basics.

Also be cautious with cases that rely heavily on discount language without explaining what is inside. Value matters, of course, but wine is not just a numbers game. If you cannot picture what kind of drinker the case is for, it has probably not been curated with much care.

Another warning sign is repetition disguised as choice. Three very similar Pinot Grigios do not create range. Nor do multiple generic reds that all sit in the same soft, jammy lane. A mixed case should broaden options, not repeat them under different labels.

Finally, presentation matters more than people admit. For a gift, scruffy packaging or a muddled product page weakens the impression before the wine is even opened.

So, are mixed wine cases worth it?

Yes, when the retailer has done the editing for you. The real appeal is not just convenience. It is having someone narrow the field with enough judgement that the case feels useful, balanced and occasion-ready.

A good mixed case gives you speed without sacrificing quality. It helps you buy with more confidence, whether you are sending a gift, stocking up for guests or simply wanting better options at home without spending an hour comparing labels. A poor one does the opposite. It turns convenience into compromise.

If you are choosing well, think less about the word mixed and more about the reason the case exists. The best bottle selections are the ones that know exactly who they are for, and make your next pour easier from the moment they arrive.
